title: The Battle of the Kraken’s Maw
subtitle: Victory, sacrifice and the water left behind
summary: The complete chronicle of the Coalition’s sixteen-hour battle in 165 EC: its opening broadsides, the fall of the Gaze of Abyss, Thulissa’s last charge and the cost of victory.
sourceNote: The complete account from the Kalvatar Discord archive, 24 April 2023. Names and events are preserved. The reading edition removes timestamps and image placeholders, corrects punctuation and typographical errors, and adds chapter headings.

chapters.title: Sixteen hours in the southern sea
paragraphs: In the dark annals of the Kalvatar Archipelago's history, there are few events that rival the sheer magnitude and devastation of the fateful clash that came to be known as the Battle of the Kraken's Maw. This brutal confrontation took place a decade ago, amidst the treacherous waters that swirl in the southern seas, where the forces of the Kalvatar Coalition bravely faced off against the largest pirate armada ever to threaten their realm. The battle raged for sixteen harrowing hours, as these bitter enemies fought tooth and nail for control of the archipelago's future. Though victory ultimately went to the defenders, the price they paid was steep, as many brave souls were lost, and the scars of the conflict still linger on to this day.

As the crimson sun dipped below the horizon, casting an eerie pallor across the waves, the opposing fleets took up their positions. To the south, a flotilla of over a hundred and twelve pirate vessels loomed ominously, their dark sails emblazoned with the terrifying visage of Admiral Blackheart, a ruthless and cunning pirate lord who had united the disparate bands of marauders under his iron fist. Among his lieutenants were the infamous Captain Shade Serpentfang, a sinister figure known for his deadly venomous blade, and Captain Sharin Bloodblade, a merciless warrior who had earned her moniker through countless acts of bloody carnage.

Facing this formidable pirate armada was the Kalvatar Coalition, a joint force of the Kalvatar Navy and the valiant Hunters, who together formed a fleet of just over fifty-six ships. Though they were heavily outnumbered, the defenders were driven by an unwavering commitment to safeguard their homeland, and they were led by some of the most celebrated heroes of their time. Among them were Captain Magnus of the Sledgehammer, a legendary Hunter whose fearsome reputation had been forged in countless battles; Captain Titania of the Iron Swan, a lightning-fast tactician who struck terror into the hearts of her enemies; Captain Johann Faust of the Jubilant, a brilliant strategist who would prove instrumental in the coming clash; and Captain Bramgard of the Crimson Tide, a fearless commander who would lead his crew to both victory and sacrifice.

Admiral Thulissa of the Trident, a woman of unwavering determination and courage, commanded the Kalvatar Navy with a steady hand and fierce heart. She was a beacon of hope for her people, a symbol of the steadfast resilience that defined the defenders of Kalvatar. Captain Falken Brightsight of the Falkoner, a skilled tactician and seasoned sailor, was known for his unwavering loyalty and quick thinking in the heat of battle. Together, these two formidable leaders inspired their troops and played pivotal roles in the defense of the Kalvatar Archipelago during the Battle of the Kraken's Maw.

chapters.title: The opening broadsides
paragraphs: The battle began with a deafening cacophony, as the two fleets unleashed a devastating barrage of cannon fire, shattering the air with thunderous roars and sending plumes of smoke and spray soaring into the sky. The Kalvatar Coalition, though smaller in number, fought with a fierce determination that seemed to surpass the pirate armada's ruthless ferocity. Led by the indomitable Admiral Thulissa of the Trident, the defenders skillfully navigated the treacherous waters, deftly outmaneuvering their adversaries and turning the very seas against them.

Captain Titania of the Iron Swan led lightning-fast strikes against the pirate fleet, her vessel darting in and out of the fray like a swift and deadly predator. Each incursion left a trail of destruction in her wake, as she deftly carved a path through the pirates' ranks, her fire-born crew's blades flashing like silver lightning in the darkness. Meanwhile, Captain Johann Faust of the Jubilant carefully orchestrated the defense, his keen mind devising strategies and tactics that would enable the Coalition to weather the pirates' relentless onslaught.

But despite their cunning and bravery, the defenders were not immune to the horrors of war. As the battle raged on, the Coalition's ranks were slowly whittled away, and even the most storied heroes were not immune to the ravages of combat. Captain Magnus, the legendary Hunter, met his end at the hands of Captain Shade Serpentfang, who struck him down in a vicious duel that raged across the blood-soaked decks of the Sledgehammer. The loss of their beloved leader sent a shockwave of grief and despair through the Coalition, but it also ignited a burning fire of determination in the hearts of those who remained. Magnus's son, Leoric, took up his father's mantle and assumed command of the Sledgehammer, vowing to avenge his fallen parent and carry on the fight for the archipelago's future.

chapters.title: The fall of the Gaze of Abyss
paragraphs: The battle reached its apex when Captain Bramgard of the Crimson Tide and his valiant crew faced the seemingly insurmountable challenge of taking down the Gaze of Abyss, a colossal warship armed with devastating cannons capable of reducing the Kalvatar fleet to splinters. Undeterred by the overwhelming odds, Bramgard and his crew fought with every ounce of their strength, managing to breach the Gaze's defenses and unleash a fiery torrent of destruction that sent the fearsome ship to the depths of the Kraken's Maw. However, their victory came at a great cost, as the Crimson Tide was left battered and broken, its decks strewn with the lifeless bodies of many brave souls who had given their lives to protect their homeland.

chapters.title: Blood, steel and the islands’ answer
paragraphs: As the battle raged on, the sky above the Kraken's Maw was filled with the thick, acrid smoke of burning wood and gunpowder, casting an oppressive pall over the desperate struggle below. The thunderous roar of cannons filled the air, punctuated by the agonized cries of the wounded and the dying, as the two sides exchanged volley after volley of deadly fire. The waves, stained crimson with the blood of countless warriors, heaved and churned beneath the ravaged hulls of the ships, as if the very ocean itself was in turmoil.

In the heat of the battle, it seemed as if the very fates themselves had turned against the defenders of Kalvatar. With each passing moment, more of their ships were reduced to smoking wrecks or sent to the bottom of the sea, their crews swallowed by the unforgiving depths. The sheer scale of the destruction was almost beyond comprehension, as the once-proud fleet was slowly but surely ground to dust beneath the relentless onslaught of the pirate armada.

But even in their darkest hour, the people of Kalvatar refused to submit to despair. From across the archipelago, vessels of all shapes and sizes answered the call to arms, their crews united by a fierce determination to protect their homeland from the ravages of the pirates. Fishing boats, merchant ships, and even private yachts were hastily converted into makeshift warships, their decks bristling with hastily-constructed cannon and their holds filled with brave volunteers, eager to lend their strength to the beleaguered defenders.

The middle of the battle was marked by a frenzy of blood and steel, as the two sides clashed in a brutal melee that seemed to defy the very laws of nature. Pirates and Kalvatar warriors fought tooth and nail, their blades flashing in the darkness as they struggled for every inch of ground. Men and women alike fought with a ferocity born of desperation, their faces streaked with blood and sweat, their eyes filled with the grim resolve of those who knew that there could be no retreat, no surrender.

The desperate boarding actions saw friend and foe alike locked in a dance of death, their limbs entwined in a deadly embrace as they fought for their very lives. The air was thick with the coppery tang of blood, the slick gore coating the decks as bodies piled upon one another. The guttural roars of the combatants echoed across the water, accompanied by the sickening crunch of bones and the wet rasp of blades being drawn across flesh.

Everywhere, there were acts of unimaginable courage and self-sacrifice, as the defenders of Kalvatar fought to hold back the tide of darkness that threatened to engulf them. Sailors leapt into the freezing waters to rescue their comrades from drowning, while others threw themselves onto live grenades to shield their friends from the deadly shrapnel. Amidst the chaos, there were countless tales of heroism and valor, as the warriors of Kalvatar fought not only for their homeland but for the very future of their people.

chapters.title: Thulissa’s last charge
paragraphs: As the battle entered its final hours, the weary and battered defenders of the Kalvatar Coalition knew that their only hope for victory lay in the defeat of Admiral Blackheart, the cunning and ruthless pirate lord who had brought this storm of destruction upon their shores. In a daring and desperate gambit, Admiral Thulissa of the Trident led a charge through the pirate fleet, her flagship cleaving a path through the chaos as she closed in on Blackheart's fearsome flagship, the Dread Sovereign.

The climactic confrontation between these two titanic figures was nothing short of legendary. Thulissa, her body battered and her spirit near breaking, fought with the ferocity of a wild beast, her every blow fueled by the righteous fury of a leader who had seen her people suffer far too much. Blackheart, for his part, was no less formidable, his years of piracy and bloodshed having honed his skills to a razor's edge. The two warriors clashed in a whirlwind of steel and fury, their battle raging across the decks of the Dread Sovereign as the ships around them burned and sank beneath the roiling waves.

In the end, it was Thulissa who emerged victorious, driving her namesake weapon, the fabled Trident, through Blackheart's black heart. The pirate lord's lifeless body toppled over the side of his ship, plunging into the dark abyss below. With his demise, the pirate armada's resolve crumbled. But this victory was a bitter one as Admiral Thulissa collapsed as soon as she returned to her ship. Her wounds were too much for her already battered body.

chapters.title: The broken armada
paragraphs: And so it was that the tide of the battle began to turn, as the Kalvatar vessels, bolstered by the arrival of their reinforcements, began to push back against the pirate armada. Slowly but surely, the defenders fought their way back from the brink of annihilation, their resolve and unity proving to be the key to their survival. The pirate fleet, for all its might and fury, could not withstand the indomitable spirit of the people of Kalvatar and the remnants of the once-mighty fleet were sent fleeing into the night, pursued by the vengeful survivors of the Kalvatar Coalition. As the final hours of the battle drew to a close, their once-mighty armada was left broken and scattered, a testament to the courage and determination of those who had stood against them.

chapters.title: What the victory left behind
paragraphs: In the aftermath of the monumental battle, the Kraken's Maw was forever changed. The once-pristine waters were now a graveyard, filled with the wreckage of shattered ships and the bodies of countless fallen warriors. The sky, once filled with the deafening cacophony of battle, had fallen silent, the only sound now being the mournful cries of seabirds as they circled above the devastation.

The survivors of the conflict, weary and battered, struggled to come to terms with the enormity of their sacrifice. Families were torn apart, leaving children orphaned and spouses widowed. The weight of loss hung heavily over the people of Kalvatar, a somber reminder of the price they had paid to protect their home.

Yet amidst the pain and sorrow, there was also a sense of pride and unity that had been forged in the fires of war. The people of the Kalvatar Archipelago, from the mightiest warriors to the humblest fishermen, had come together as one to defy the seemingly insurmountable odds, and in doing so, they had forged a bond that would endure for generations to come.

In the years that followed, the story of the Battle of the Kraken's Maw would be passed down through the ages, a tale of tragedy and triumph, of courage and sacrifice. The memories of those who had fallen, like Captain Magnus of the Sledgehammer and Admiral Thulissa of the Trident, lived on in the hearts of their loved ones and in the annals of history, their names forever etched in the chronicles of the Kalvatar Archipelago.

For the survivors, the scars of that fateful day would never truly heal, a constant reminder of the horrors they had faced and the friends they had lost. Yet in their grief, they found solace in the knowledge that their sacrifices had not been in vain, that their homeland had been saved from the clutches of the pirate scourge. Together, they vowed to honor the memory of the fallen, to rebuild their shattered lives, and to ensure that the lessons of the Battle of the Kraken's Maw were never forgotten.

And so, the people of the Kalvatar Archipelago turned their gaze towards the future, their spirits buoyed by the indomitable strength and resilience that had carried them through the darkness. In the echoes of that great and terrible battle, they found not only sorrow, but hope: the hope that one day, the scars of war would fade, and that the people of Kalvatar would rise once more, stronger and more united than ever before.

title: A Midsummer Gala
subtitle: A palace on the sea, and a garden out of earshot
summary: Reinhardt Holst comes to Lord Mortimer Vanris’s floating gala as hired security. Hyacinth Alastor comes for the pastries. Between the ballroom and the garden, both find more than they expected.
castNotes: Lord Mortimer Vanris, Lady Cassandra, Lady Syra Delamont and Lady Arabella Thornwood also appear in this account.
sourceNote: The supplied text of A Midsummer Gala, arranged into nine scenes. The dialogue, interior thoughts and events are retained, with one grammatical correction. This edition ends where the supplied text ends: Reinhardt identifies the Blue Bolts across the hall.

chapters.title: A palace for one night
paragraphs: Lord Mortimer Vanris had built a fortress on the sea for one night's party, and his advisors had not stopped complaining about it since the keel was laid.

It floated a mile off Goldwind: the Vanris Floating Pavilion, all galleries and lantern-hung decks and ballrooms with glass roofs, with a garden in the middle of it, real grass and real trees, that had cost more than most islands are worth. It could hold ten thousand guests, Lord Mortimer said. Every noble and merchant in the archipelago had been invited to the midsummer masquerade to count them.

At sunset the lanterns came on, thousands of them, and the whole thing lay on the water like a jewel someone had dropped. Boats came out from the harbor in a long glittering line. Music, laughter, the smell of spice and roasting meat, the clink of more glasses than anyone could count. Behind the masks, everyone was already counting something else.
Reinhardt Holst came aboard with the staff, not the guests.

Lord Mortimer had asked for him by name, as an enforcer for the night, and had offered a sum Reinhardt could not afford to turn down. Everyone understood the point of it. The disinherited son of House Holst, the youngest Gold in the Hunters, standing at a Vanris door like a hired dog, where every family in the islands could see him do it. Reinhardt understood it too. He had bills a vendetta runs up, and he had taken the money.

He wore the jacket. Armada blue once, dyed black now, the collar high. His sister's sword hung at his hip and her pistol at his belt. He walked the halls without a mask, which in that place was the same as wearing a sign, and he watched the crowd the way he watched a horizon.

There was nothing here he wanted. A world that had looked the other way when he needed it was dancing in front of him, and he did not have to like it to work in it. He only had to keep his eyes open. A party like this was a battlefield with better food.

chapters.title: The Pink Lady arrives
paragraphs: The Pink Lady of House Alastor came to perhaps one gala in twenty, and the host who got her bragged about it for weeks.

Nobody ever knew why she chose one invitation over another. Hyacinth was not sure she knew herself. She did not come to dance, or to be seen with anyone; she came to eat, drink, listen to the gossip, and leave the moment she was bored, which was usually in the middle of somebody's speech.
The doors opened. A soft mist of pink petals drifted in over the nearest guests, and there was no herald, because none was needed.

Her butterfly mask hid nothing. Her gown was long and pink and sewn with flower sequins that seemed to stir when she moved, and its long sleeves fell behind her like a cape; there were butterflies on her shoes. Her hair was braided in a pattern that had taken two people an afternoon. Hyacinth did not blend in, and did not try to.
She looked over the room and named the bad disguises one by one, until her eyes stopped on a man with no mask at all.

She did not know his name. She knew at once that he did not belong there, and she began to go through the list of who he might be. It was not her habit to hide that she was looking at someone, so she did not. For the first time in a long while, she was curious.

Reinhardt felt the look before he found it. Across the hall, through the crowd, was a woman in pink who outshone every jewel in the room, and she was not looking at the dancers. She was looking at him.
He should have stayed at his post. He had not been given one.
He crossed the room to her.
"Good evening, Lady Hyacinth," he said. "Forgive my boldness, but I can't help wondering what brings the Pink Lady to an affair like this."

Her head turned fast, and her eyes went wide. There were rules at these things. She was meant to have time to walk the room, get a drink, and take a plate of food before the host greeted her and the crowd started on the introductions.

"You greet me before the host," she said, not quite to him; she was thinking aloud. "And though we have never been introduced, you use my first name. No. Boldness is not the word." She found it. "Rude."
It was not an accusation. It was a fact, like the weather.
Her eyes went to his sword, to the pistol, to the guests around them who were trying very hard not to stare at him, and failing.
"Hunter," she said, annoyed, though mostly with herself for taking so long.
Reinhardt realized, with a jolt, that his hand had half lifted toward her, as if to check she was real. He put it down. People were looking. He hated people looking.
"I," he said. "You. I am rude." He found his footing, and something like a smile. "Perhaps I'm thinking of taking you into custody. For suspicious behavior." He touched the shackles at his belt.
If he had already wrecked his chance of an ally, he could at least get a laugh out of it.
He did. It was small, and it showed her fangs, and behind her the tip of a pink tail swung from side to side.
"Suspicious behavior? I would be in custody forever."
"MAGNIFICENT!"

The voice came from everywhere at once; it had been made louder with magic. Lord Mortimer Vanris came through the crowd like a ship through small boats, a big man in a bigger costume, and took Hyacinth's hand and showered it with compliments. Without her, this would have been a dull party, and they both knew it. Then he looked at Reinhardt, and smiled.
"Is our enforcer giving you trouble, my lady?"
"Not at all, my lord," said Reinhardt. "I was only admiring Lady Hyacinth's attire."
"Then why don't you go back to your post, and leave the important people to talk about important things?"
"You didn't give me a post, my lord." Reinhardt bowed, far too deeply. "I'm here to look for threats." He stayed bent long enough to enjoy it. "My apologies for my rudeness, milady."
He walked away. He got three steps.
"This is not Mangalar Port, boy," Lord Mortimer said, loud enough for half the hall. "You're only working here."
Reinhardt kept walking.

Hyacinth watched it all with great attention. She did not mind the praise; her entrance had been short, but it had worked, and Vanris was one of the few houses she preferred to keep amused. She was more interested in the other thing. Was the scorn because of the man's rank, or to impress her, or something else? Whatever it was, it had done her a favor: the whole hall was whispering now, and she had not had to lift a finger.

"Lord Mortimer," she said, "this is indeed not Mangalar Port. Nobody told me of any change to your security, and I believe proper introductions are in order." She held out her arm toward the hunter's back. "Only then will I consider an apology."
She looked at Mortimer and left a silence. It was his place to make introductions.
Reinhardt turned around. Before the lord could find his words, he stepped up and took the moment himself.

"Lady Hyacinth, Lord Mortimer. Allow me. Reinhardt Holst, enforcer for this magnificent gala, here to see to the safety of the guests." He met her eyes, and this time the bow was a real one. "I apologize for earlier. I'm honored to make your acquaintance."
Lord Mortimer's face did several things at once. "Very well, Holst," he said. "Carry on."

chapters.title: A woman in the doorway
paragraphs: Reinhardt found a wall at the edge of the hall and leaned on it.
"Since when do you keep company with devils?" said a woman's voice beside him, dry and amused. "Should I be jealous?"
"Cassandra." He did not look round. "I never took you for the jealous kind."

Lady Cassandra was Lord Mortimer's spymaster, though her lord did not know half of what she did. She stood with her back to the room and passed him an envelope without looking at it. "Thank you for your help with the southern campaign, Lord Reinhardt. House Vanris hopes it can still count on you."
"Your master is being very loud tonight," said Reinhardt, and put the envelope away. "And I'm not a lord."
"He is," Cassandra agreed, with a sigh that had years in it, "very special."

Across the hall, with a plate of lemon and blueberry sponge cake and her mouth full of it, Hyacinth watched the two of them talk. She could not hear a word, but she had a sense for one particular kind of woman.
"Make sure her drinks go flat," she murmured, "and her food goes bitter."
The shadow at her feet stirred, once, and was still. It was a small curse. In Hyacinth's opinion, a deserved one.

chapters.title: The wives by the mirror
paragraphs: The music changed, and dancers went out onto the floor. A famous painter had set up an easel by the windows, and Hyacinth noticed with some satisfaction that most of his canvases already had a pink figure somewhere in them. She was tempted to ask Lord Mortimer for one, to wave at her mother the next time her mother complained she was never seen anywhere.

Then she slipped out into the garden, where nobody was, and threw herself down on the grass, plate, glass, and all. Something she could not see caught them on the way down and set them gently beside her.
She lay there and made her plan.

Tonight she would let herself be greeted, far more often than she liked, because she was listening for one subject: a campaign at sea, either just finished or about to begin. The wives would be the key. Wives were wonderful. They never knew the important details, and they always let slip something they shouldn't, out of the sheer excitement of a husband about to sail or just come home. The captains and admirals would come later. They would be careful around an Alastor, but as the night went on the drink would make them brag. That was for later.
For now, the wives. The more scandalous, the better.

She found them in front of a great gilt mirror: a knot of jeweled women, flushed with wine, talking low and checking over their shoulders. In the middle of them, a woman with fiery red hair was telling something that made the others lean in.
The hair looked familiar. It occurred to Hyacinth, for perhaps the first time in her life, that not paying attention to people could be a disadvantage.

She walked straight past them to the mirror and ignored them completely. She tucked away a few strands the grass had pulled loose, and made sure her lavender horns showed through her braids. They were the only part of her that proved she was her father's daughter, and she was proud of them. It was bait. She hated it. It worked.
"Lady Hyacinth, isn't it?" said the red-haired woman, at last. "You look stunning tonight. We so rarely see you. Are you always this drawn to mirrors, or is it something more?"

"Drawn? It's a beautiful mirror. But I'd rather not have grass in my hair, or be taken for a sunburnt human." Hyacinth turned to them. "But that isn't what you're asking me." She saw no point in pretending. "I think what you share is valuable. It would be a foolish mistake to call your conversation gossip. A convenient mistake for some. We both know better."
She smiled with every one of her fangs. "Forgive me. Hyacinth Alastor. A pleasure, Lady...?"

She let the gap hang, and sipped her drink, and listened under the words. Now that she had said her own name, they were all thinking of her, and thoughts that are already turned toward you are easy to hear.
"Lady Syra Delamont," said the red-haired woman, after a moment. "Wife of Lord Delamont." And one by one, the others gave their names: the wives of men who mattered.

Delamont. Of course Lady Syra was worried. The east was her husband's domain. Hyacinth had a vivid memory of exactly what she had been doing while her tutors explained the eastern houses to her: running off to a lesser party for raspberry tarts and some proper sparring. A small lesson was forming in her mind, and it went something like *perhaps sea business is important.*
"We were speaking of the trouble to the east," said Lady Syra. "Trade routes cut, unrest among the people. Something large is happening, and we're all worried what it will mean."
"I can only imagine," said Hyacinth, and meant it; having someone at sea is never easy. "Things have been a little unsettled."

*It's a disaster*, was what she wanted to say. But Lady Delamont looked as fiery as her hair, and if House Alastor ran out of its ridiculous imported flowers because of Hyacinth's mouth, Hyacinth would have to leave the country and change her name.
Lady Syra smiled at her, a little conspiratorially, and the others relaxed. They talked of disrupted shipments, of families split by the closed routes, of the fear going through the coastal towns.
Then Lady Arabella Thornwood, wife of a famous admiral, leaned in.

"My husband swore me to secrecy. But I think it has to be said." She lowered her voice. "He says it's one ship. One ship doing all of it. A black ship, with red sails. It comes out of nowhere, strikes, and is gone before anyone can follow. It leaves no survivors. The few who've seen it say there's something on board, as if the ship itself were cursed."
The women were very quiet.

"Only one ship is known to have faced it," said Lady Arabella, "and that was the young Holst's. Corina's brother. The gods keep her." Several of the ladies made faces. The young Holst, by their faces, was a noble gone wrong, one of those unruly hunters that plague the sea.
Hyacinth's tail wanted to wag like a puppy's. She held it still.

"That sounds terrifying," she said. "Your husband must be a brave man." That was not flattery; the sea frightened her, and something that could move on it like that frightened her more. "Hunters can be a necessary evil. I know them well." She smiled. "Perhaps that explains the choice of guards tonight."
"I wonder," said Lady Arabella, and looked across the hall to where Reinhardt stood, "whether that's a coincidence."
"I've never known Lord Vanris to be a man of coincidences," said Hyacinth, and stirred the pot on purpose. "For a party this size, I'd bet every detail was planned. Except for me, of course."

They would be talking about her and her family by morning. She let them. She had a larger question now. The hunters were the only thing standing between the coast and that ship, and Lord Mortimer had treated the one who had faced it like a dog. A host showing off his guards for her was nothing new. This was something else.

chapters.title: Moonlight in the garden
paragraphs: The music slowed. The middle of the hall cleared for a dance, and for one minute the music took Hyacinth completely. She closed her eyes and swayed.
When she opened them, she was surrounded.

Every bachelor in the hall had come, and every bachelor's mother, and old officials, and nobles, and several men who had no business asking anyone to dance. Some waited to catch her eye. Others simply announced themselves. She said "No," and most of them went. Some did not. Each time she had to say it again, it came out harder: "I do not want to dance with you, and it is in your best interest to accept that and leave."

None of them knew that a public refusal was the least of it. For weeks after, every one of them would be very slightly unlucky. Caravans that left a few minutes early. Favorite pastries sold out. Shoes that pinched. Milk that turned. Each day would lose one small pleasure, and none of them would ever know why.
And still they pressed in. Too many hands. Too many voices.

Under the floor of the hall, the shadows began to spread, slow and thick, like tar. Her throat was closing. *What's a proper party without a little murder?* she thought. *Didn't you want a show, Lord Vanris?*
She was a breath from doing it. Every one of them.

Something cracked high overhead. One of the great silk curtains tore loose from its rings and came down, in a long slow wave of fabric and dust, over a crowd of officers. There was shouting, and swearing, and Lord Mortimer's magic-loud voice raging above it all, and the musicians, to their great credit, never missed a note.
A hand closed around her wrist.

It pulled, firm and gentle at once, and she went with it, through the crowd and out, and the shadows came with her, and for a few seconds everyone on the Pavilion was in more danger than they had been all night.

When she knew where she was, she was in a dim passage at the edge of the garden. A few dozen shadows stood ready to take her rescuer's head off. Her own arms were black with them to the elbow, and her hands were set as if she held a sword.
"Are you all right?"
She knew the voice. She let the breath out, and every shadow around her let it out too.
"It wasn't me who needed saving," she said. She was angry, and there were angry tears in her eyes, and she turned her face away so the hunter would not see them.
"I know," said Reinhardt. "I'm saving them from you."

He had seen her face in the crowd. He led her through a gap in the hedges into the inner garden, where the noise of the party sank away into leaves and the small sounds of hidden things, and the moonlight came down green through the branches.
"Will I have to put you in cuffs for real?" he said.

Hyacinth laughed, though she was still not looking at him. "As long as we're clear." She wiped her eyes with the edge of her sleeve. She unbuckled her shoes, and a shadow took them and carried them at her side, and she walked barefoot in the grass, touching the leaves as she passed them like a curious child. "It's a little murder, my dear hunter. Don't be such a prude." She held out her wrists. "But I suppose it is your duty. If the occasion arises, you're welcome to try. The night is young, and we can't let your dear patron have a dull party."
He did not answer that. He took a handkerchief from his pocket, cherry pink, of all colors, and held it out.
She took it without a word, and kept it. She would not try to give it back until much later.
"I've no objection to a little murder," Reinhardt said. "I was thinking of some myself, after the toast. I'm sure Lord Vanris wouldn't mind, as long as people talk about the party for days."

"After the toast? Classic. A little old-fashioned for my taste." She sat down in the grass and looked back at the lights of the Pavilion. "But nobody invites an Alastor to a party without planning for a murder or two. You'll be fine."
"So you're going to satisfy my curiosity?" he said.
"You saved my dress from some messy stains. I might."
The teasing went out of his face.

"I was wondering," he said, very quietly, "what someone like you is doing in a place like this." A faint smile came back. "Besides the Faewild honey-glazed lotus pastries, and the best elderberry wine in the east."
Hyacinth let the question sit. Her head was light with wine, the music was far away, and there was grass under her, and for the moment she felt something she almost never felt in company: free.

"The Pink Lady of House Alastor at the grand gala," she said, mocking. "Whatever could she be doing here? Well. I'm sorry to disappoint you, but food and drink are more than enough. Put Faewild pastries and elderberry wine in an invitation and it's a bribe, and not a subtle one." Then, in a series of voices, each worse than the last: "Oh, you have your mother's looks and your father's swordsmanship, what a disaster if it had been the other way round. Your mother's garden. Your father's army. How is Nemeia? How is Valthor?"
She stopped.
"Isn't someone missing," she said, "from all that praise?"
It was a trick question. For once in her life, she wanted someone to get one right.
Reinhardt took his time.

"Perhaps," he said, "what they miss is the person under the title. The woman behind the Pink Lady." His voice was low. "And perhaps they miss that she'd rather have the moon and an empty garden than all their lanterns and noise."
Hyacinth laughed, and frowned, and smiled, all at once.

"Don't be so presumptuous, hunter. It would be foolish to think you understand me after a few words." But she sounded more pleased than scolding. "Don't draw false conclusions from true impressions. That goes for more than me." She looked down at her gown, for a moment caught by her own vanity. "I don't mind the parties. Or the dancing. The dressing up is impractical, but sometimes. The music, the food, the drink. I'm sorry, but there's nothing special about what I like."
She was quiet for a while.

"You're not supposed to enjoy them," she said, looking at the party, not at him. "And I resent being shown nice things I'm not supposed to have." She gave him a sideways grin. "So I do as I please, and I enjoy as I please."
It was not true of tonight. She had not done one thing all night as she pleased, and she could feel it on her face.

"Presumptuous? Me?" said Reinhardt. "You've caught me, my lady. But from the little I've seen, you find joy where nobody else would think to look. In a place like this, full of empty manners and hidden knives, you still manage to enjoy yourself." He said her name, "Hyacinth," quietly, as if it were a private word. "And tonight, it seems, you were pleased to escape the crowd and sit under the stars with a presumptuous hunter. Not the usual way to spend a gala." He raised his glass. "To doing as we please. And to finding joy where we don't expect it."
"REINHARDT HOLST!"
Lord Mortimer's voice, of course.
Reinhardt rolled his eyes. "Excuse me, my lady. Duty." He lifted a hand and went.
Hyacinth heard every word that followed. Her ears were better than he knew.
"There you are, Holst. Where have you been?"
"Looking for dangerous people, my lord," said Reinhardt, knowing perfectly well she could hear him. "We may be in danger at this very moment."
Lord Mortimer laughed it off. "Just do your job. Have you seen Lady Alastor?"
"Of course, my lord. Who could miss her?" A pause, long enough to be cruel. "Oh. Did you mean, do I know where she is now?"

Hyacinth stood. She raised her glass toward where he had been. She was already deciding whether to murder Lord Mortimer where he stood, and settled instead on giving him the worst hangover of his life from every wine he drank tonight. It would put him off his favorite vintage for good. A dozen bottles of it, from a very well-known merchant, would go over the side in the morning.
When she came out of the hedges, her hair was perfect, her shoes were on, and her face looked as if she had just arrived.

"There's no need to guard my whereabouts," she said, "though I do appreciate it." She turned to her host. "Reinhardt not only rescued me from the crowd, Lord Vanris, he was kind enough to keep me company while things calmed down. The quality of your guards. I know I shouldn't expect less, and yet I keep being impressed." She watched to see which word of praise annoyed the lord most. "He was telling me how my family's shipments have fared with the hunters at sea. The sea isn't my thing, but I can't help being curious. Though surely we can agree a conversation like that wants good food, and a refill."

Lord Mortimer could not refuse her. "Hyacinth, my dear, always a sight. I'm glad you're well. And thank you, Reinhardt, for looking after our guest." He did not like saying it. "Holst, fetch us another bottle of the Sunhold vintage. It goes beautifully with the main course." And to Hyacinth, smiling: "In the meantime, may I steal a moment of your time? There are things I've been meaning to discuss."
He wanted to know what the Alastors were up to, and he thought she would tell him.
"Wine sounds lovely," said Hyacinth. *But not with you.*
She looked at the hunter as he turned to go, and put a few words straight into his mind, as gently as she knew how:
*Don't take too long. But let him talk.*

Reinhardt checked for half a step. Not from fear. He had heard of what House Alastor could do. He had never felt it, a voice laid into his thoughts as lightly as a hand on a sleeve. He nodded to her, very slightly, and went.

chapters.title: Wine, whispers and crystals
paragraphs: "You don't waste any time, Holst."
Cassandra, in a doorway, out of the light.
"You're as hard to find as a ghost," said Reinhardt. "Ever thought of joining the living?"
"Where's the fun in that?" She took a glass of red from a passing tray, sipped, and spat it straight back. "What in the name of every tide is wrong with the drink at this party?"
Reinhardt held up the bottle he had found, a far better one. "Perhaps your palate isn't used to Lord Vanris's taste."
"Laughing at a lady's expense is very ungentlemanly, Holst."
"And lurking in doorways is very ladylike, Cassandra."

In the garden, Hyacinth paced while Lord Mortimer talked. Part of her mind was still in the hunter's, like two people lingering in a doorway after saying goodbye; she could feel his amusement, his curiosity, and she felt guilty for spying and warm that she was still on his mind. Then Cassandra filled his thoughts, and just like that, Hyacinth was out.
She thought about sending a shadow after them. She did not. Something about Cassandra told her the woman would notice, and would not be amused.

"Lady Hyacinth," Lord Mortimer was saying, all honey. "I've been curious about your family's recent interest in the University. The Alastors are known for their wisdom, but scholarship seems a novel venture."

*He can't be this stupid,* Hyacinth thought. Her walks with Nemeia through the University's halls were hardly a secret. Did he think no one knew, or were his sources that bad? It was sloppy. She would have expected this from Cassandra, quietly; if her lord was asking it openly, caution had gone out of the window. *Novel.*
*Oh,* she thought. *He can be this stupid.*
And something lifted off her shoulders.
The clink of bottles. Reinhardt was back.
"I hope I'm not interrupting anything important," he said. "But the party was running low on good taste."

"It's the downfall of every party," said Hyacinth, and held out her hand for a glass, and only just remembered not to have her shadows carry the bottles; she had already given the poor hunter a voice in his head tonight, and she was not ready to frighten him off. "I'm thrilled you're so interested in scholarship, Lord Vanris. But I'm afraid I'm the wrong Alastor to ask."
"Holst," said Lord Mortimer, sourly. "Your timing is impeccable as always."
"If I didn't know better, my lord, I'd think you weren't glad to see me. A party without good wine is a night without stars."
The lord swallowed it. He turned back to Hyacinth, and something urgent came into his face.
"Lady Hyacinth. A recent shipment of crystals from the south. Connected, I'm told, to a band of mages from Crystalmaw City. Have you heard anything about it?"
Reinhardt's face did not change. But he had been following a trail of exactly those crumbs for months, and it had led him to this party, and he had not expected to hear it said out loud by the host.
"Surely, my lord," he said smoothly, "that's a conversation for wine, not whispers."

Hyacinth had hoped her host had some sense left. His desperation surprised her. She was a foolish girl to him, she knew; she was almost never seen in her house's business. But even she knew that knowledge is earned, not handed out.

"Crystalmaw is no place for a lady, Lord Vanris," she said. She quietly undid a curse she had laid earlier; this wine had better be good. "And the sea is cursed. Too cursed even for me." To her, it was simply a fact. "Plenty of houses and merchants deal in crystals. Throw a stone anywhere here and you'd hit someone in the trade." She tried to read the hunter, and could not. If this had Lord Mortimer worried, Cassandra was two steps ahead, and the hunter's charm was part he played for the gala, and now she wondered whether he played it for her too. "But you seem to think my house is involved. Is that it?"
She let it hang. She took the bottle from Reinhardt and read the label. It was very good, and very strong. She would have to drink it slowly.
She did not.

Reinhardt filled their glasses. "Too many people in the crystal trade," he said, looking at Lord Mortimer, and the lord seemed to shrink a little. "It does make things complicated." He raised his glass. "To good conversation. And better company."

chapters.title: All she needed was a boat
paragraphs: The talk went back to small things for a while, and the wine went down, and Hyacinth found herself laughing more than she meant to, with her cheeks hot. She hoped the drink was working on Lord Mortimer faster than on her. She was not sure it was.
*You don't make strong wine stronger,* she thought. It was a lesson she would never learn.
"Lord Vanris," she said, not bothering to steady her voice, and took a step toward him, and stumbled, and caught herself on Reinhardt.
He caught her. His arms came round her without his asking them to. For a moment they were closer than they had been all night, and he could smell her perfume under the wine.

"Lady Hyacinth," he said, low, for her alone. "The wine may be a little strong for you." The smile stayed, but his eyes were worried. He set her on her feet, and his hands stayed a moment longer than they needed to.

Hyacinth registered everything. Calloused hands, rough, holding her very carefully. The cloth of his jacket. That he smelled clean. She let it last longer than she should have, too. For weeks afterward she would find herself going back over it, whether she meant to or not. Officially, she had stumbled on purpose. Anyone who asked would be told so.

"Lord Vanris," she said, in a loud whisper, "forgive me, I have to ask. Is House Vanris in need of any help?" She did her best to look concerned. "It's only gossip, of course. But I'd never forgive myself if you needed a hand and I didn't offer mine."

Lord Mortimer's mouth tightened. "Dear Hyacinth, you're very kind. But I assure you, House Vanris is stronger now than it has ever been." He took another glass from Reinhardt; the hunter's bottle seemed never to run dry. "All our ventures are doing splendidly. Including our new acquisitions in the south. The crystal market down there is booming, and with our new partnership with a certain order of mages in Crystalmaw City, we're very well placed to take advantage." He leaned in, pleased with himself. "I'll tell you a secret. Those crystals aren't just for mages. They have other uses. Some of our biggest buyers are other noble houses. You'd be amazed at the demand."
He laughed, as if he had told a joke. Nobody else did.
Reinhardt went on pouring, smiling, and missing nothing.

"What wonderful news," said Hyacinth, in the voice she used to get things out of her father. "How mean of you to keep it to yourself. You know House Alastor always keeps an eye out for House Vanris. These new houses, they're nothing I need worry about? And the crystals sound so wondrous. Tell me more."

She knew those crystals. Krysta. She had only ever handled it under Nemeia's watch, and only refined, polished, tamed, nothing like what it must be in the raw. Even so, it had sung to her. She had had to be pulled away from it.

"Worry, my dear? Not at all." Lord Mortimer settled back in his chair. "Magnificent in the raw. Beautiful. Alive. The southern houses are as wild as the land they come from, but nobody mines and refines it like they do. And the Alastors have always had a taste for rare things." He poured himself more. "You've never seen anything like it."

Word by word, he laid out a web that ran from the mines of the south, through houses nobody had heard of, back to the great families of the Heartland. To him it was trade. Reinhardt, beside her, could see it was a great deal more than trade, and from the stillness of Hyacinth's tail, so could she. They looked at each other once, and understood each other perfectly.
Hyacinth had made up her mind. There were things she would have to see for herself.
All she needed now was a boat.

chapters.title: An invitation and a threat
paragraphs: Lord Mortimer moved on to the northern families, and Hyacinth's attention moved on to the hunter turned wine-steward.

She had a burning question, and a few smaller ones she would ask anyway, partly because of the wine and mostly because she wanted to know. Any other night, the sensible answer would have been to have his head off. Alastors do not ask questions like hers. Any hint of betrayal is dealt with before anyone has the chance to lie, and there are no trials, and Hyacinth believed in family tradition, when it suited her.
The thought had not crossed her mind once.
Every murderous wish she had tonight was already spoken for: the rude guests, some for the lord in front of her, one saved specially for a woman in a doorway. None for the hunter.
She realized she had been staring at him for far longer than was polite, and that he had noticed. She laughed at something the lord had said.
"You seem very interested in something, Lady Hyacinth," said Reinhardt, and offered her another glass. "Can I help?"
She was blushing, and the night hid it badly, and not even pink skin could hide it at all.

"Well," she said, under her breath, so only he could hear. "Unlike our noble host, I don't like an audience." She raised her voice for the lord. "Perhaps we should go back to the party, Lord Vanris? Before anyone worries. Or worse, gets the wrong idea about where we went."
"Lord Vanris," said Reinhardt, "your guests will be missing you."
Lord Mortimer could not say no without a scene. "Quite right. The night is young, and there are toasts to be made."
As they walked back into the noise, Reinhardt leaned toward her. "I think a more private conversation would do us both good."

Her heart was racing. She put it down to the wine, and the politics, and her sudden new need to travel by sea. If things had been even a little different, she thought, he would have had bite marks he could never explain.

And under all of it, anger. Anger at the thought of betrayal, and anger at the thought of her, Hyacinth Alastor, charmed by a former Holst, and worse, a hunter. She was smarter than that. And yet there he stood, with his head on his shoulders, all ten fingers on his hands, and not a single curse on him.

She walked fast into a knot of merchants and nobles, and by the time the two men caught up she was in the middle of them, all teeth and sweetness. "Oh, I only had to see the gardens, my mother would never forgive me if I didn't describe them, and Lord Vanris, ever so gallant, had to make sure I was all right." The lord was too vain to see the bait. In no time he was telling his own version of the story to anyone who would listen.
Hyacinth slipped away to the emptiest corner of the hall, and looked back once at the hunter. It was an invitation. It was also a threat.
He followed.

chapters.title: The Blue Bolts
paragraphs: Her shadows ran out from her feet and drew a ring around them both, and the noise of the party went flat, as if someone had shut a door.
"Words won't leave this circle," she said. "We can speak freely."
She was not usually this careful. Tonight, more than anything, she wanted to be wrong.

"Hunter," she said. "No longer a Holst, and just as charming. It's not unusual for good company to try its luck with me at parties like this. Sometimes, like you, they even get to enjoy it." Her eyes were hard, and her face was flushed, and the wine was making her sloppy, which made her angrier. "But I'm not the only one who's enjoyed your charm tonight, am I?"
The shadows gathered at her feet, at her fingertips.

"We have a friend in common. She said my name a while ago. She has a nasty habit of saying it wrong." She smiled. It was not a nice smile. "You've spent the night going back and forth between the Pink Lady and Lord Vanris's little spy. You greet the Alastor everyone thinks is the naive one, the spoiled one, the pink one. You go to Cassandra. You come back to me, just in time to hear our host spill his secrets." Her arms were folded. Her tail had wound itself tight around her leg. "Convenient."
"State your business with Cassandra, Reinhardt. Have I charmed you into a string of coincidences? Or have you been trying to do the same to me?"
He did not step back.

"I won't deny any of it," he said. "You, Lord Vanris, Cassandra. Each for its own reason. My business with Cassandra is an old arrangement, born of need, not trust. We share some interests. Our paths cross, the way two rivers might, for a while, before each goes its own way." He came a step closer. "With you, I wasn't trying to trap anyone. I was curious. And I've found I like your company more than I expected. My loyalty is hard to earn. Once it's given, it doesn't move. Tonight, my interest has been in you."
*Hunters,* Hyacinth thought, *and their water metaphors.*
Her tail loosened a little. Not all the way.

"That's very nice," she said. "It's also not what I asked, is it?" She rubbed between her eyebrows, and waved off a few of her shadows, which left with what looked very much like relief. "So what would it take to earn your trust, Hunter Reinhardt? Because what I need right now goes a little past that."
She walked a slow circle in the small space she had made.

"I'll trust you this much. I won't pry into whatever river you and Cassandra are sharing, as long as you can promise me it doesn't touch me, or my close family." She came close, closer than was proper. "You see, I can't lie to them. They know my lies too well. And they wouldn't hesitate to take both our heads at the faintest hint of treason." Her fangs showed at the corners of her smile. "I'm very fond of keeping my head on my shoulders. And I have to admit, I've grown fond of yours."

"It has nothing to do with you, or with House Alastor," said Reinhardt. "Directly. Not at the moment. Our dealings are strictly professional." Something in her face told him what she thought of the word *professional* where Cassandra was concerned. "I understand the price of betrayal, my lady. And for what it's worth, I've grown rather attached to your head too. It's made this evening a great deal brighter."

A small crowd of shadows came hurrying in through the dark, carrying plates and glasses and cups, and lemon cakes, and lemon tarts, and lemon everything, stacked one on another. Half the menu had been planned to lure the Pink Lady, and she had not been able to eat any of it all night.

"Manners, hunter," said Hyacinth, as he reached for a plate. "You're in this space with me. Don't make a beginner's mistake and think the shadows serve anyone but me." She waved a hand, and the shadows set the food down. "Of course I asked for enough for both of us. I do have manners."
Reinhardt noticed, with great amusement, that certain drinks and certain sweets drifted out of his reach whenever his hand went near them.
"Your servants have excellent taste," he said, and took a lemon tart, one of the few he seemed to be allowed. "I have to say, the sweets are the second-best thing here."
Then his eyes moved, very slightly, past her shoulder, and he lowered his voice.

"You've been collecting admirers since you arrived. But that's nothing new for you, is it?" He tipped his head, barely, toward a group of men across the hall, who were not dancing, not drinking, and not dressed for a party, however hard they had tried. "Those ones, though. Those are the Blue Bolts. An elite company, out of the Goldmanes in the south. Very efficient, and not the kind you want taking an interest in your plans for the evening."
He took another bite of the tart.
"Though I doubt," he said, "that it's only your charm they're interested in."

title: Between Shadows and Ice
subtitle: Kiel Keyron, Noel, Caelan Caelius, and Serrah of Hadari, a coal-mining village of the Icy Expanse, in the months a shadow was taking its hunters.
summary: A shadow has been taking Hadari’s hunters for months. Kiel Keyron, Noel and Caelan Caelius find refuge with Serrah; kindness, fear and the arrival of Ninthalarion bind their roads together.
castNotes: Serrah of Hadari takes a central role in this account. Yuran, Oleg, Erik, Jonah and Zari also appear.
sourceNote: The five chapters supplied by Kafeii on 2 November 2026, replacing the withdrawn incomplete roleplay extract. Paragraphs, dialogue, interior thoughts and scene breaks are retained; events between the supplied scenes remain off-page. Two height references follow the author’s later correction of Ninthalarion to about 2.10 meters. The account ends where the supplied text ends.

chapters.title: Hadari
paragraphs: The wind found every gap in Kiel Keyron's furs on the last mile to Hadari.

He had come a long way to be this cold. He had sat for days in the library at Goldwind, with books that came apart when he turned the pages. He had gone south to Jakupur, to the few people in the White Flame who would still talk to him. Every road they pointed him down ended here: a coal-mining village at the top of the world, so far from anything that it did not have an inn.
People watched him come in. Nobody waved. A woman pulled a child indoors by the collar. Two men by the mine road stopped talking, and started again, lower.

What they were saying, he gathered fast. People had been going missing for months. Hunters went out and did not come back. On nights without a moon, someone always swore they had seen a figure at the edge of the lamplight, darker than the dark around it.
A man named Yuran, whom the village thought odd, gave him a bed. Kiel thanked him, laid out his tools, and went back out as soon as the light went.

He found tracks in the snow that started nowhere and ended nowhere. He found marks scratched into the stones at the mouth of the mine, and they were not miners' marks. And the whole time he had the feeling, which he had learned to trust, of being looked at by something that did not blink.
He was standing at the edge of the village, thinking about that, when the two lights came out of the dark.
Noel had been following them for a long time.

They were souls, two of them, small and glowing, and they had been lost on the tundra when she found them. She could not get much out of them. They had been hunters. Something like a shadow had caught them out on the hunt and squeezed until there was nothing left. They wanted to go home. That was not an ending anyone deserved, so she had decided to keep them company until they could rest.
*Hurry up,* they said. *The shadows keep growing. Do something about it.*

She could not feel the cold any more, but she remembered how it had felt. She remembered breath, too: the little cloud of it that should have gone up from her mouth. Sometimes other things came back, warm rooms and soup and people around a fire, but the faces would not hold still. Everything was blurry.

She looked back once at the long line of her own footprints, and wondered what she was doing out here. Then she saw that a second line of footprints ran beside hers. Had it always been there? It went on ahead, so she followed it. It led to a town.
The two lights shook with joy and danced around each other. Noel smiled. Maybe she had done something good. She did not remember, but it was nice to see them happy. It suited them.
Kiel watched the girl walk out of the snow with two souls bobbing at her shoulders.

She was small, and too thin, and wrapped in bandages under clothes that had belonged to several larger people. Her hair was mostly white, with streaks of black in it, as if the white had come late. She leaned on a staff of grey, petrified wood. Under her hood, only one eye showed.
Something about her was wrong. He could not have said what. He let his hand rest near his sword.
"Greetings, traveler," he said. It came out harder than he meant it to. "It seems we've both been drawn to this village. My name is Kiel Keyron. Tell me who you are, and what brings you here."

She blinked at him, as if he had that moment stepped out of the air. The two souls were fading. She lifted a hand without looking at it, and a small green light went out of her fingers and into them, and they brightened and bobbed on. Necromancy. Kiel had seen it before, in worse hands.
She sighed with relief. Then she gave him a slow little wave.
"Oh. Hello. I think I'm lost. Who are you? My name is Noel. It's nice to meet you."
"Kiel Keyron," he said again. "A traveler, of sorts. It seems we're both a little lost here."
That cheered her up enormously.
"Oh! So we were traveling together?" She came closer, friendlier now. "I'm sorry to ask, but where are we again?"
"No, Noel. We just met. This is Hadari. A mining village. Coal. People here keep to themselves."
"Oh. We just met." She kicked at the snow. "I'm sorry. My memory isn't what it used to be. It's actually very bad."
The souls drifted over and hung in front of Kiel's face, as if they were having a look at him. Noel nodded along to something he could not hear.

"They want to see their families," she said. "Something swallowed them. Some kind of shadow. They just wanted to go home, so I brought them here." She turned and looked at the dark houses, the shut windows, the corners the lamps did not reach. "Don't you feel something watching us, Ki... Kie... ah. Friend?"
"Kiel," he said. "And yes. I feel it too."

"Kiel! Yes." She pulled a small, worn book out of her coat and wrote in it with a stub of charcoal: his name, the place, and, after some thought, *friendly*. One of the souls pushed itself onto the page to get her attention, and she laughed.
"All right, all right. Let's take you home."
She set off into the village after it, slipping on the ice and catching herself on her staff, without another look at him or at the watching dark.
Kiel saw then that no breath came out of her mouth at all.
He went after her.
The soul led them to a house, and Noel knocked.

The door flew open at once. The woman behind it had been waiting for somebody, and for one moment her whole face was relief. Then she saw what was on her step. She screamed, and slammed the door, but not before one of the souls shot past her into the house.
Noel had been about to introduce herself. She held her staff a little tighter against her chest.
What was she doing here again?
Kiel put a hand on her shoulder, and spoke through the door, slow and even.
"Please, don't be afraid. We mean you no harm. The one who just came in is yours. He's come home. We're here to help him rest, not to bring trouble on you."
He believed that, mostly. It was the best he understood of it so far.
After a while the door opened again, a little, and then all the way.

The house was full of a hunter's life: pelts on every wall, elk horns over the hearth, a skinning knife on a nail. The soul had curled itself up in a big, worn leather chair by the fire, the kind of chair that has taken the shape of one particular man. The woman looked at it, and away. Then, because she did not know what else to do, she gave her guests something hot to drink and put more wood on the fire.

Noel held the cup in both hands and looked into it as if she had never seen one. When the fire caught and roared, she shifted on her stool. Then, while nobody was looking, she moved the stool a little farther from it. Then a little farther.
The woman sat down across from them. She had not slept properly in a long time. It was in her eyes, and in her hands.
"Tell me what's going on," she said. "And what that thing in my husband's chair is."
Noel brightened.
"Oh. He says he lives here."
The woman stared at the small, bandaged girl as if she had been slapped.
Kiel said nothing. He laid a hand on the woman's shoulder, lightly, and let Noel lead. After a long breath the woman's shoulders came down.
"That's my husband," she said. "Isn't it."
Noel looked at the soul in the chair, and nodded.
"He says he missed you."
The woman put her hand over her mouth to hold something in.
"Can he understand me?"
"Yes."
She lifted Kiel's hand from her shoulder, and stood, and went to the chair. The soul rose to meet her.
"He says he loves you," Noel said. "And he's sorry you fought, the last time you saw each other. He really didn't mean to call you a..." She frowned. "A fat lump of coal?"
The woman made a sound that was half a laugh and half something else.

Then it all came out of her at once. She was sorry about her cooking. She was sorry she had called him a smelly oaf. She was sorry about the times she had locked him out for going hunting without telling her. She was sorry, she was sorry.

"He says he's sorry too," Noel said. But there was too much to carry back and forth, and she kept losing the thread of it. So she turned her hand over, and it filled with that green light, and the soul in front of the woman grew.

It lost brightness as it grew, and gained a shape, until a rugged, bearded man stood on the hearth rug. He was mist. You could see the fire through him. But he was smiling at her, and he looked at peace.
She reached for his face, and her fingers went through it.
Noel saw that, and frowned, and sent one more pulse of green out of her palm. The man thickened, a little. When his wife reached out a second time, his hand closed on hers.
They held on to each other for a long while, and said things too quiet for anyone else. Then he stepped back, and nodded to her, and came apart into small glowing bubbles, and was gone.
The woman looked at the place where he had stood. Then she folded down onto her knees and wept.

Noel stood there, stricken. That had not been part of the plan. It should have been obvious, perhaps. She took a pelt off the nearest chair and put it around the woman's shoulders, and rubbed her back in small circles, and did not know what else to do.
Kiel had stayed in his corner. He had watched it all, and he was turning it over.

He had seen necromancy used to make slaves of the dead. He had never seen it used like that. The girl walked a line between light and dark, and walked it carelessly, like a child on a wall. And she forgot. Who forgets like that? Someone with a hole in her head, or someone whose head somebody else is keeping empty.
He decided he would watch, and learn, and be ready.
Someone pounded on the door hard enough to shake it.
"Serrah! Are you all right? You're in there with those strangers, aren't you? Let us in!"
There was a mutter of agreement behind the voice. More than one man.
For one moment Kiel thought about how quickly he could empty the street. Then he put the thought away, where he kept the others, and went to the door.
He opened it a hand's width.

There were seven of them, and most of them looked worn to the bone. They carried picks and splitting tools from the mine, and a couple of torches. The one at the front was a giant of a man, with a hatchet in his fist that was the only well-kept thing about him. The steel shone.
"Serrah is safe," said Kiel. "There's no need for this."
"Then why is she crying?" said the giant. "Huh?"
"And there's a witch. We *saw* her!"
"Are you in on it too?"
"Maybe if we kill the hag, it all stops."

Half of them would not meet Kiel's eyes. A few shuffled their feet. But they loved their village, and their neighbors, and that was stronger than whatever they saw in his face. Behind them, down the street, people stood in doorways and at lit windows, watching. One more push, Kiel thought, and the whole village goes up like dry tinder.

"Listen to me," he said. "I understand. But violence won't fix this. Serrah is grieving. She's crying for someone she lost, and that's all." He held the giant's eyes. "The one you call a witch has a gift. She can give comfort to people in pain. She isn't your enemy. I have no intention of letting harm come to any of you. Stand down, and let's end this quietly."
The giant looked at him for a long moment. Then the hatchet came down.
"We'll be watching," he said.

He waved, and the others went with him. They huddled in the cold a little way off, whispering, looking back, and then they broke up and went home. All but the giant. He leaned against a woodshed across the street, folded his arms, and did not take his eyes off the house.

Inside, Serrah was still crying, and had taken Noel as a handkerchief. She held the girl in a crushing hug and wiped her eyes and her nose on her. Noel smiled awkwardly, and patted her every few seconds, and did not complain.
Kiel shut the door.
"Noel," he said. "Where are you staying tonight? I'm at Yuran's. He's an odd one, but he's kind."
Noel looked at him with nothing at all in her face.

Serrah lifted her puffy red eyes. "If you like," she said, and sniffed, "you could both stay with me. I wouldn't mind." She sniffed again. "What would you like to eat? I've got a good potato and meat stew on the fire."
Noel looked at Serrah, and at Kiel, and at Serrah. Then the other soul was in her face, swelling and flaring, pointing at the door. *Outside. Now. Now.*
"Ah," said Noel. "I don't know. I think I should go? I think I have things to do?" She began to untangle herself from Serrah, badly.
"If you have somewhere to be," said Kiel, "I'll go with you. We can come back once we know what this one wants."
"No."
Serrah was on her feet, and there was fire in her eyes.

"You've got to be out of your mind if you think I'm letting you out after what just happened. Have you seen what time it is? And look at her!" She waved a hand at Noel. Small, too thin, too pale. She looked sick, or starving, or both. Serrah put a palm to her cheek, and drew in a sharp breath.

"She's freezing! The poor thing!" She turned a look on Kiel that put the whole blame on him. "I insist. And I'm not taking no for an answer. Come on, girl." She steered Noel toward the soft chair in the corner. "What was your name again?"
"Ah. I think it's Noel?"
The soul gave something very like a huff, and swelled a little more.
"Very well," said Kiel. "For a little while."

He went to the small window and stood beside it, where he could see out without being seen. His breath fogged the glass, and faded. Across the street, the giant with the hatchet was still there, a shape against the woodshed, watching back.

Serrah put Noel in the chair and buried her in pelts. Then she pushed the chair right up to the fire, to warm her. Noel looked at the flames in horror. When Serrah turned to stir the pot, Noel scooted the chair back an inch. Then another.
Serrah handed Kiel a bowl of stew without asking, and went back to fussing over the girl, still shocked at how cold she was.

"How did she get all of these injuries?" She was tugging at the bandages. "Did she fall off a cliff? It's absolutely ridiculous, the state she's in. What have you people been doing?" She gave Kiel the look again. "You should be doing a better job of keeping your friend safe."
"I don't know much about Noel," said Kiel, and ate a spoonful. "I found her tonight, same as you."

Serrah looked at him for a moment. Then she nodded, slowly, and turned back to Noel, and her voice went soft, the way a mother's does. Where was she from? Why was she out here? How did she feel? Did anything hurt?
"I'm okay," said Noel. It was all she ever said.
Serrah bit her lip. "Well," she said. "How about we take a look at those injuries, all right?" Over her shoulder: "Don't you go taking a peek, young man. Understood?"
She did not wait for an answer. She started on Noel's shoes. They took a long time to come off, as if they had frozen to her. When they did, every inch of skin under them was purple and black.
Nobody said anything.

Serrah began to unwind the bandages on Noel's legs. Under them were open wounds, still letting out a little blood. More frostbite. Bruises. Cuts that had barely closed. And there was no smell of rot, none at all, and nowhere on her, not anywhere, was there a single scar.
At about that hour, a long way out on the snow, a man was talking to himself so that he would not stop walking.
"A fortnight," said Caelan Caelius, into his scarf. "A fortnight of white, and the wind howling all night. No rations left. My legs will give out any time now. And my ears." He felt them. "Going."
He braced against a rock while the wind tried to take him off it.

There had been talk of a village past the ice fields, beyond the peaks. Folk had gone missing there. Nobody knew much more. But the traveler he had met in the last town had sworn that something was wrong in that place, that something had taken root there and meant to stay. Caelan had met all kinds of people on his pilgrimage, rich merchants and poor fishers and farmers, and he had never seen a man's face as troubled as that one.
So he had made it his business.
He had not seen a single animal in days, he realized. No tracks, no birds. As if everything that could run had run from here.

The wind dropped, all at once. The clouds pulled apart. Moonlight came down and turned the whole country blue, and under a sky full of stars he saw a scatter of cabins and shacks not far off, some of them in pieces, some of them barely standing, with lamplight in a few windows.
"This must be it," he said. "I shall press on."
Kiel saw him from the window: one figure, wading through the blue snow toward the village.
He put down the bowl and went out to meet him.
They stopped a few paces apart. Neither of them said anything for a while. The wind whispered along the street.
"Who are you," said Kiel, "and what brings you here?"
The stranger pulled his scarf down. He was young, and tall, and auburn-haired, and so tired he swayed.

"Nothing more than a traveler on a pilgrimage," he said. "I help the people I find in need, and keep in check the ones who disturb the peace of those less fortunate." He looked past Kiel at the village. "Are you the one in charge here? I could use a little rest. And some warmth."

"I'm not in charge," said Kiel. "But your arrival is... curious. We've had our share of trouble here lately. You'll forgive me if I find it hard to trust strangers right now. You say you came to help. How do we know that?"
The man did not answer that. There was nothing to say to it, and he seemed to know it.
Kiel let out a slow breath.
"You can stay the night," he said. "But I'll be keeping an eye on you. If you turn out to be a threat to these people, I won't hesitate."
He stepped aside.
Across the street, the giant with the hatchet watched them both.
How many strangers, Kiel wondered, could a village this frightened take in before it did something about them?

chapters.title: The Axe
paragraphs: The spirit died screaming, and Serrah's house went with it.

When it was over, Kiel stood in what was left, breathing hard, while the last of that high, thin sound faded out of the air. The sun was going down. It laid long red shadows across the snow and turned the smoke orange. He felt it, then: the fierce, clean lift of a fight won. He turned to share it.
Noel and Serrah were on the ground.

There was blood around them, a great deal of it, bright on the snow. Over them stood the big man with the hatchet, who had been on their side a moment ago. His eyes had gone wild. The blade he kept so carefully was wet.
The spirits that lived in Noel's clothes flared up around her and threw themselves at him. Men were running from the houses. Kiel's hand had already gone to his belt.
He drew out an old sigil, and woke the dark that slept in it, and spoke.
*"Halt."*
The words came out in a tongue older than the village, and a cold wind came with them, and everyone in that street shivered at once. The big man slowed, as if he were wading through deep water.
"This madness ends now," said Kiel. "Let them go."
The hatchet shook in the man's hand. He did not lift it again.
Caelan came limping out of the smoke, scratched all over, with a shallow gash across his back. He had been at it since morning. They all had.
"Is Noel all right? Tell me she's unhurt." Then he saw the blood. "Kiel. How did this happen?"
He shoved his way through the villagers to get to her.

The men had the big man by the arms now, and were dragging him off. He went stiff as a post. People were around Serrah, asking if she was all right, looking at the gash in her back. It was deep. She was white to the lips and holding on to the nearest arm with both hands.
Noel lay a little way off, looking toward Serrah's blurred shape, hoping she was all right.

She could feel her blood going out of her. Her small hand moved down over her belly and found that it was cut through. She could not move her legs. Her fingers went in, through meat and bone, and found out why. Her legs were not attached to her any more.
It was all a dull pain. It usually was. She blinked, slowly. That was the only thing that showed she was not a corpse. She coughed up some blood, and kept her eye on Serrah.
Caelan went down on his knees beside her, and something in his face gave way. He had sworn to keep this girl safe. He should not have left her alone.
He tore his cape off and pressed it to the wound. It was too deep. There was nothing to press against.

"Is there anything you can do?" He was asking the spirits, which hung frozen in the air around her. "Please. I beg of thee. Help her, as she has helped all of us." His eyes were wet. He passed the cape under her, and wrapped it around, and held it there.
Then he looked up at the villagers who had called her a witch.
"Are you happy now? What did she ever do to you? Nothing! She only wanted to help your lost ones, and look how you've paid her!"
None of them would meet his eyes.
Noel blinked a few times, until Caelan's face came clear.
"Are you okay?" she said.
The spirits floated around the two of them and did not answer. Serrah was being carried off. The people left in the twilight looked at their boots.
Noel put a small hand on Caelan's cheek. Her fingers were stained with her own blood, and as cold as midwinter.
"I'm okay," she said, and gave him a soft smile. She coughed a little blood every time she spoke. "It's okay."
Kiel was spent. He turned a cold look on the villagers.
"Your ignorance and your fear did this," he said, through his teeth. "We came to save you from what's been preying on this town, and you turned on the people who helped you."

Then, to Caelan, more gently: "Keep pressure on her wounds. I'll find a way." And to the spirits, in the voice he had used on the big man: "You owe her. She freed you from what was tormenting this place. Now help her."
He went to Serrah. The two people holding her let him through without a word. He tore a strip off his own shirt and pressed it to her back.
"Stay with me, Serrah," he said, low. "We've come this far together."
There was one vial left on his belt. The liquid in it was white, and it shimmered. He put it to her lips.

She did not sip it. She drank it all at once, the way a drowning person takes air, and then she let out a long breath, and he felt it under his hand: the edges of the wound drawing in. She looked up at him.
"Thank you."

Caelan held on to Noel, and began to hum. It was the tune they had sung in the clearing deep in the woods, three notes and back again. He hoped it eased her. He looked across at Kiel tending Serrah. He had not even seen that she was hurt.
The night came in. One by one the stars came out over the black, as if another fight were starting, against how thin a thing a life is.
"Stay with us," Caelan said. "It isn't time to go yet." *Hm, hm, hm, ooh.*
"Your singing is pretty," said Noel. She ran her thumb back and forth on his cheek, to soothe him. "Just don't move me, and I'll be okay. All right?"
"You're welcome," Kiel told Serrah, and managed a smile.
Then his body sent him the bill for the day. Every bruise. Every cut. Every blow he had taken since morning. His breath went ragged. The stars blurred.
His legs folded, and he went down on his back in the snow.

The cold came through his clothes and did nothing for the pain. He lay there looking up at the sky, and asked whatever gods might be listening to watch over these people, these friends he had not meant to make.
Caelan would not let go of Noel's hand.
"I won't move you," he said, "or leave your side, until I'm sure you're out of danger. This I vow."

He gave the villagers one more look, and they felt it. But he knew, under the anger, that their fear was natural. Outsiders are feared, and shunned. Serrah had taken them in, and that had put a mark on her, and she had paid for it with her house and everything in it. It was all gone with the smoke.
Serrah had got herself off the ground. Her bruises still showed, but she was out of danger. She went to Kiel where he lay and rolled him over.
"Jonah," she said, to a middle-aged man nearby. "Help me get him inside. He's earned that much."
Jonah nodded, and he and a neighbor picked Kiel up by the arms and legs.
"Serrah, please keep him company," said Caelan. He could barely hold himself upright. "I'll stay here with Noel."

The spirits had begun to move. They gathered over Noel, small glowing lights in the dark, and pressed themselves down into the wound in her body, mending what they could, paying her back for her kindness.
Noel giggled.

"I'm supposed to be helping *you!*" She squirmed. "Stop it!" And she laughed out loud, delighted, as they went through her. They grew smaller as they worked. After a while they settled down beside her, dim and tired.
