She looked guilty about it. But she had her small, grateful smile on, and she did not look as if she hurt at all. She looked up at Caelan, still trying to comfort him.
"It's going to be okay."
In the corner of the yard, two villagers stood holding shovels. They had brought them to bury her. They looked at the girl, and at each other, and at the shovels, and did not know what to do.
Halfway across the yard, Kiel woke up to find himself being carried like a sack of flour.
"Hey! Hey! I'm not a baby!"
His face went red, from the effort or the shame of it, and he wrenched himself loose and stood. He wobbled. He was plainly hurt. He ignored it with great determination.
He stumbled over to the two men with the shovels.
"That," he said, with a strained smile, "won't be necessary."
They took a step back from him.

He went back to Serrah and looked her over, frowning, pressing gently around the wound, watching how fast the edges were closing and how much color was coming back into her face. The brew was working. He wanted to see it work.

"Yes," said Caelan to Noel. "It's going to be okay. I've no doubt of it. We'll rest soon. I'm going to try to move you." There was a smile in his voice again. To the spirits, he said, "Thank you for not leaving her alone. You should be able to rest too, once this is over."
He checked that the bandage he had made was firm, and not too tight, and ruffled her hair. Then he looked up at the people still standing in the dark.

"People of Hadari. I know it isn't easy to have strangers barge into your lives and ask for your trust. But we have a duty to keep you safe, and to root out whatever has been hurting you." He was so tired his voice shook, and he kept it level anyway. "I only ask for your hospitality, once more. A place to rest, and to tend our wounds."
They began to murmur among themselves. They had treated these strangers badly, and some of them knew it.
The two men with the shovels put them behind their backs.

Serrah, the pain gone, was herself again. She rounded on the nearest neighbors and practically barked at them to get a place ready for these kind people, right now. They jumped. Within minutes they were moving food, and blankets, and even beds.

Noel felt her legs coming back. The tired spirits climbed up and propped themselves on her chest, so they would not be left behind. She looked at the sky for a while. Then she looked at Caelan, and her face drooped.
"What are we doing here again?" she said. "You look tired. Did something happen?"
"We're going to go and sit by a fire and rest," said Caelan. "And you can tell us your story."
He knew that lost look by now. She forgot. She forgot all the time. To live in the moment was a fine thing, he thought, but not to be able to keep any good memory at all was a hard one.

"Where do you come from?" He gathered her up in his arms and got, slowly, to his feet, with whatever strength he had left. His clothes were soaked in her cold blood. It did not bother him. "Do you have a family?"
To the men with the shovels he said, politely, "You won't be needing those. Could you show us the way, and find her a change of clothes?"

"A fire?" Noel scrunched up her face. "I don't really like fire much. Can't we go somewhere else?" Then she looked down, and saw his cape, which was red through. "Oh no. Is that... did I do that? I'm so sorry. I'll clean it up later, okay?" She looked up at him, terribly sorry, as if she had spilled soup on it.

His red hair was familiar. His face was nice, and he was being nice. She was sure she knew him, but no name came up. She tried to think about a family, about a home. Little memories rose, and popped like bubbles: faces she could not describe, places she could not name. But she knew one thing, deep in her bones. She had been walking for a long, long time.
"I don't think so?" she said. "I walk. Yes. I walk. I walk a lot. But I can't remember where."
The men with the shovels nodded hard and hurried off, whispering about how ridiculous it was to go looking for clothes for someone with one foot in her own grave.
People stared as Caelan carried her through the crowd.

Old Yuran gave them his house, a big one at the very edge of the village, up against the forest, and the village thought him peculiar, but it was glad of him tonight. Little Zari, a girl with very determined eyes, followed Serrah everywhere, carrying whatever she was handed. Nobody wanted to be alone, so people gathered in and around Yuran's house, and someone started a pyre, and someone else started a pot, and everyone put into it what little they had.
It was not a celebration. The creature was not gone, only driven off. But for one night they were not alone with it.
Serrah had changed toward Kiel. She did not say so. She brought him things before he asked for them.

Caelan followed her through the house, thinking. The girl in his arms forgot. She hid from the sun. She would not go near a fire. There was something living in her that was beyond him, and he knew it, and he did not mind.
"Would you like to keep walking with me and Kiel?" he asked her. "I have a feeling that if we stay together, we can look after each other."

Noel tipped her head to one side. Her one eye began to shine. She did not remember who this nice man was, or who this Kiel might be. But the idea of being part of a group made something ache in her, sweetly.
"I think I'd like that," she said. There was a long pause. "It sounds lovely."
"You can lay her down here," said Serrah, and showed them a narrow bed in the corner, with a little table beside it: bread, dried meat, a glass of water and a jug. Blankets were piled on the chair.
Caelan laid Noel down carefully. She made sure the spirits did not roll off her chest.
"Serrah, could you help her change her clothes, and her bandages?" he said. "Noel, I'll wait outside."
Serrah went white. She looked at all the blood, and the pale little girl, and her face twisted.
"Ah. I'm not sure. I'm not really a doctor." Her voice climbed. "What if I accidentally peel something, or touch something, and she just... she just..."
She turned and almost ran to Kiel.
"Excuse me. Maybe, perhaps, do you have another vial of that wonderful medicine you gave me? Your friend. I don't know what to do with her. Perhaps that would help?"

She could practically hear a clock ticking off whatever time the girl had left, and the weight of it on her shoulders felt like enough to kill her too. On the bed, Noel was rolling the little spirits around under her palm like marbles, without a care in the world.

Kiel had been looking for a place by the door to lay his head. He had heard Caelan ask the girl to stay with them. It sounded fine. It was not for him. He had too much to keep hidden for that. Something passed over his face, and was gone.
"That was my last one," he told Serrah, and gave her a smile with nothing in it. "I'm afraid I'm spent." He looked over at Noel. "But I've a feeling she'll be all right."
He was not sure of that. He said it anyway.

Caelan went outside and knelt in the snow. He scrubbed his hands with it, and then his arms, and then took more and wiped the blood off his face. He opened his hands and looked at them, and spread each finger.
"These hands," he said, to nobody, "are meant to protect the ones who can't protect themselves. The ones circumstance has put on the short end of the stick."
He looked up at the stars.
"We lead by example. Always."
Then he walked to the house where they had shut up the man with the hatchet. He knew that vengeance can feel like justice. He had decided long ago never to let it in.
A few men stood guard outside the door. They looked at him with doubt, and a little fear.
"It's a sad thing, what happened today," Caelan said. "But the worst has passed, and nothing that matters was lost. Serrah is well, and the girl will recover."
The men looked at each other.
"We don't know why Oleg did it," said the one on the left. "He was always bitter. Always bickering. But he never went this far before."
Caelan kept a careful distance from the door.
"Maybe the fear got the better of him. For now, please keep him inside, until the village as a whole decides what to do with him."

They mumbled apologies. On his way back he found the two men he had sent for clothes. They still could not understand how the girl was alive and kicking. They handed him a worn grey dress and a matching cowl against the cold, which had belonged to a woman's daughter, three winters dead. Then they disappeared as fast as they decently could.

He went back slowly, and stopped to talk with everyone he passed. He listened to what they were afraid of and what they hoped for. Most of them were helping to build up the pyre, and they looked at him the way people look at a lit window. Some asked what they could do. Their hands were rough from the mine and had never held a weapon, and they had all watched Oleg go down like a felled log and rave like a madman. So they did what they could. By the time he got back to Yuran's he was carrying pelts, and a basket of dried meat, and had turned down three offers to wash his shirt.
He told every one of them that the worst had passed.
Inside, Serrah had Kiel by the hand, begging him at least to watch while she tried, because she was terrified of making one wrong move and killing the girl.
And Noel was humming her three notes again.

She knew how low she was. Maybe she had helped a lot of people today. But she looked at the little souls lying on her, dim and tired, and she knew she was not done. So she gathered up what she had left, and pushed it at them, to give them a little more.
They froze, and then they bounced away from her as hard as they could go.
They were trying to make her heal herself. She did not know that. She blinked after them, very, very confused.
Caelan came in with his arms full and set it all down by the bed, the dress on top.

"You shouldn't be using your gifts, Noel. You need to rest, and heal." He saw Serrah's face, and went to her and took both her hands in his, and looked her in the eyes. She had been through a great deal, and it showed.

"Thank you, Serrah. Words can't say how grateful we are. You let us into your home, and then you risked your life protecting Noel. I know thanks aren't enough to repay that. I'll be in your debt for the rest of my life." He nodded at the chair. "Sit. I'll take care of things here."
Then he turned to the man in the corner, whom he had quarreled with on the first night, and trusted now.

"Kiel. We need to get our strength back, while we have the chance. And then I'd like us to join forces, and make sure the village and everything around it is truly free of what we faced today." His voice was serious. "I've no skill with these things. But with what you know, and my strength, and Noel's gift with spirits, we can stop another day like this one." He let that sit. "Please, give it some thought."
Kiel gave him a faint smile. A noble way to see the world, he thought. Maybe a naive one. He wished the world had more people in it like Caelan Caelius. Then maybe he could stop expecting the dark.
He looked at Serrah, who was still wringing her hands, and had an idea.
"Perhaps you could help me instead," he said. "I could teach you a little medicine. First aid. You can practice on me."
She hesitated, and then she nodded.

They took a lamp to a quiet corner, and he showed her how to clean a cut and how to dress it, and how tight a bandage should be, and how to tell when a wound was going bad. His body gave her plenty to practice on.

It was stiff between them at first. It did not stay that way. He told her about some of the places he had been, the fights, the lives he had saved and the ones he had not, how hard the world was out there. She listened with her eyes wide, half horrified and half hungry for more. Then she told him about life in Hadari: the winters, the mine, her husband, everything she had come through, and how she had kept going anyway. They laughed sometimes, and sometimes they did not.
By the time they were done, her hands had stopped shaking. When she smiled, Kiel thought, she looked younger than he had taken her for.

Across the room, Caelan took off his breastplate and set it by the wall with his bow and quiver. He took out bandages, a pot of honey salve, and a cake of beeswax. He had his own cuts to see to. He saw to hers first.
"Noel, I need you to stay still while I look at your wounds. If it hurts, just say, and I'll stop."
He wet a cloth and began to wipe the dried blood off her arms, and her legs. Some of it had got onto her face.
Noel looked up at him. Without even thinking about it, she put her hand on his arm, and the green went into him.
His cuts closed. His bruises faded. Strength came back into him, like something hot to drink on a cold morning.
She let out a sigh, more tired than ever, but satisfied. Her eye seemed to lose its focus, and she lay back and stared at the ceiling.
The spirits flickered among themselves, outraged. Had they given themselves for nothing? What was *wrong* with this girl?

Caelan understood then. She had no regard for herself at all. Spirit or living, she could not stand to see someone hurt without taking it on, as if it were her own, and she would empty herself to do it.
He put his arms around her and held her, his hand on her hair, her face against his chest.
"Please rest, Noel," he said. "Maybe you can't help it. But if you keep using this gift with nothing held back, you'll wither away."

Then he went on. He cleaned every cut he could find. Honey on each one, against festering. Beeswax over the honey, to help it close. A bandage over that. Again, and again, until she was patched from head to foot. He took his ruined cape away, and covered her pale skin with pelts and blankets. The spirits drifted in circles above her while she looked at the ceiling.

Kiel found a free corner and sat down in it, his back to the wall, his legs out. The room was quiet now, except for the rustle of blankets and the murmur of Caelan talking to the girl. He shut his eyes.
There was something warm in his chest that he did not have a name for any more. It had been gone a long time. He fell asleep before he could decide what it was.
Late in the night, the village settled. Out by the pyre the wood cracked and settled, and a few people still sat up drinking and trading stories. In the little room, an oil lamp burned low.
Caelan kept watch over his friends while they slept. When he was sure Kiel was deep under, he took one more pelt and crossed the room with great care, and laid it over Kiel's chest.
"Relentless warrior," he whispered. "Let the night lighten your burden, a little. Let you forget, for a while, the dark secrets you keep so close to your heart."
Most battles, he thought, begin and end inside a person. Quiet wars, fought between what you believe and what the world is.
He made himself a place by the window, where he could see the stars over the moonlit snow, and wondered what was coming for them. Then he was asleep too.
Kiel stirred when the pelt came down on him, but he did not wake. The warmth of it went into him. His brow, which had been knotted, came smooth.

He dreamed of old fights, and of the faces of people he had lost, and for a while it was more than he could hold. Then, in the middle of it, something steadied. There were other faces in the dream: a knight, a girl, a widow with a bandage in her hands. The dark that usually filled his nights drew back from them.
He woke at first light, with the morning coming in at the window, and saw them all still asleep around him, and smiled. It was a small smile. It was real.
Noel had not slept at all. She had lain all night looking at the ceiling through her eyelashes, without a single thought in her head.

Serrah woke up cheerful. She had a pot of hot soup going before anyone else was up, and asked each of them how they felt, and whether they had slept well, and whether they needed anything, because if they did, she would settle it with the rest of the village, just tell her.
Then she stood over the pot with the ladle in her hand, and looked at them all.
"So," she said. "What's the plan for today?"

chapters.title: The Back Window
paragraphs: Ninthalarion had been dead for a very long time. Then Noel had raised him, and now he was walking out of the forest with them, a little over two meters of Frost Elf, naked, grey to the bone, covered from head to foot in the Xylothara's ash, and putting one foot down after the other as if each one had to be argued into it.
"Assistance," he was saying, "can be part of any bargain."
He looked Caelan over, and then Noel, and seemed to weigh them. Then he nodded.
"I can do that. It would be more than fair, I believe."
"Then we agree," said Caelan. "We'll help you until you can fend for yourself. It's the right thing to do."
He wondered, privately, whether it would have gone so easily if the elf were not so weak.

Noel kept stopping. Whenever Caelan looked back, she was crouched in the ash again, arranging the remains they passed, or she had turned around to go back and do it some more. After the fourth time, Ninthalarion sighed. He reached down without breaking stride, took a fistful of the back of her cloak, and lifted her off the ground like a coat off a hook. Her feet dangled.
"There," he said. "We will be faster now."

"Aren't you cold?" said Caelan. The wind coming through the dead trees cut like a blade, and the elf did not seem to notice it. "We'll have to cover you up at some point. You can't go around dangling things in that state without proper clothes."
Ninthalarion looked at him as if he were slightly stupid.

"I am quite literally a Frost Elf. We do not heed the cold's will or its desires. If anything," and he scratched himself with the hand that held Noel, so that she swung about like a rag doll, "the ash is the irritating thing here."
"We should try to get out of the forest before dark," said Caelan. "I haven't seen any animals near here. I don't want to push our luck."
The spirits came floating around them. As soon as Noel had stopped swinging, she nodded at them.
"Ah. They say we should go into Serrah's house by the back window." She scrunched up her face. "The village doesn't like Frost Elves?"
Caelan sighed.
"What I mean," he said to the elf, "is that you should cover your loins. It's a matter of decency. You don't mean to stay naked forever, do you?"

"Of course not." Something moved in the elf's chest, small and muffled. It might have been a laugh. "I will find vestments when I can lay hands on them. If it bothers you so much, perhaps you can share some textiles with me."
And the corner of his mouth twitched. It was very slight. It was the smallest smile Caelan had ever seen on anyone, and it was there.
"What do you know of Hadari?" Caelan asked. "Its people. Would they welcome you, if you were there?"
"Hadari." Ninthalarion thought about it. "No. I do not recall anything named Hadari. If there are humans there, then yes, they would be wise to fear me."
Noel had forgotten why she was in the air. She began, very earnestly, to brush the ash off him. He held her out at arm's length, where she could not reach.

Caelan laughed. "Well, we've got a pelt or two at the house. That'll cover your noble parts." Then, more seriously: "I don't think anyone should fear you or hate you, unless you give them a reason. But be mindful of the people there. They haven't had it good, for a long time."
He remembered when they had said the same thing about him.

Yuran's house stood at the very edge of the village, where the forest began, so they only had to circle around through the snow mounds to reach it unseen. As they got close they could hear Hadari: people talking, lively now, gossiping about food and the mines and whether the two young adventurers ought not to marry some of the girls here, really, they could do worse.
Ninthalarion shrugged at what Caelan had said, as if it had taken him this long to think about it.
"Humans are weak, and quick to run. It would be natural, and wise, for them to be wary of me."
They reached the back of Yuran's house, with a great deal of effort, and there was the rear window.
"Let go of her," Caelan whispered, and held out his arms, and took Noel. Next to the elf she looked like a doll. "Come here, Noel. I'm going to open the window and let you in. Try not to fall over."

He looked behind them. Nobody. He took hold of the sill and eased the window open. The murmur of the village came across the snow. He lifted Noel by the waist and set her down inside, gently, and she stepped back to make room.
Then he looked at the elf, and at the elf's enormous body.
"Let's see if you can squeeze through, my friend."
Ninthalarion looked at the window for a long time without moving.
"I have terrible doubts about this," he said. Then: "Let us break the frame."
"We can't break it. Wait until dark and try the front door. I'll bring you some pelts meanwhile."

Caelan went in first with half his body, careful not to bang his armor on the frame, then a leg and an arm, holding tight, and then he was through and standing beside Noel. He found some of the pelts the villagers had given him and passed them out.
"Cover yourself with these. And don't make any noise."
"Hmph."

The elf took the pelts and sat down in the snow, and let out a long, exhausted breath. Then he began to scrub himself with handfuls of snow. The thought of Xylothara dust on his skin was not to be borne.
Noel looked at Caelan with an excited smile.
"Now what?"

"Now we wait, and see if we can get the others to accept him too. For now he has to sit outside. At least he won't be cold." Caelan glanced out at the pale shape in the pelts. "Let's find Serrah and Kiel. I hope they've got some strength back."
He reached for the little book in her pocket and turned to the last pages. There were drawings there, if you were generous: a woman with a ladle, a man with a sword.
"This is Serrah," he said. "And this is... Kiel. They're our friends. They're staying here with us."
Noel looked at the drawings as if they were the most wonderful thing she had ever seen.
"Oh. Oh, okay."
They went through the house to the bedroom. Serrah and Kiel would still be resting, Caelan thought, or should be. The fire was down to embers, and the room was warm.
"Let's check," he said, and opened the door.
The point of a sword was at his throat before the door had finished opening.
Kiel had moved before he knew he was moving. Years of waking to danger had done it for him. He stood very close, and his eyes were not friendly.
"I could have killed you," he said. It was a low sound, like a warning from a dog. He kept it quiet, because Serrah was asleep. "Why are you sneaking?"
His eyes went past Caelan, to the back window, and the huge pale shape crouched in the snow beyond it.
"And who is *that?*"
Caelan did not flinch. He looked down at the blade, and then up.

"I was being mindful of your rest. Yours and Serrah's." He put his hand on Kiel's sword hand and moved the blade aside, unhurried, and pointed with his eyes at what he had brought home. "I didn't want to interrupt any smooching that might have been going on in here."
Kiel did not lower his guard.
"I brought a guest," said Caelan.
Noel looked from one of them to the other, frozen. Wasn't this man a friend?
In the quiet, from the bed, came the sound of Serrah snoring.
Kiel's face changed. Something in it let go, and he almost smiled. He lowered the sword.
"Dangerous business," he said. "Can't say I blame you for being careful. Just announce yourself next time. All right?" He glanced back at the bed. "She was very tired. Let's keep it down."
Then he went to the window and looked out.
Out in the snow, the Frost Elf sat wrapped in a borrowed pelt, scrubbing at his arms with handfuls of snow. He was too tired to lift his head. Even sitting, he was taller than the woodpile.
Kiel looked at him for a long time.
"Where," he said at last, "are we supposed to put him?"

chapters.title: Erik
paragraphs: In the end Serrah let the elf stay. She had been afraid of his kind every day of her life, and she said yes anyway.
Not long after, Kiel Keyron came out of a cave at dawn with a boy in his arms.

The cave had been cold. Out here it was colder. He pulled his cloak tighter around the child. Whatever Noel had done in there, the boy was breathing now, against Kiel's chest, small warm breaths. He had not been breathing when they found him.

Noel walked beside him. Kiel thought about what was coming. What the village would say. What Serrah would say. Most of all, what this had cost the girl, and how much of it she was carrying on those small shoulders, whether she knew it or not.
"Keep an eye on him, Noel," he said, low, and nodded at the boy. "We'll need to find his family when we get back. They deserve to know what happened."
The first light was coming through the trees, laying gold on the snow. Below them the village was still asleep. Kiel's breath smoked.
"We've got a long day ahead of us," he said.
He did not say the rest. They were bringing a life back. A second chance. Maybe, he thought, it was a second chance for them too.
Noel scrunched up her face.
"I don't like the sun."

It was plain that this worried her more than anything else about the morning. She had no idea what she had just done, or what would come of it. She wanted a little hole to hide in until it got dark again.
The boy was mumbling, shivering, saying names. Where his house was. Who lived there.
Kiel looked down at her. He did not understand it, but he did not need to.

"All right, Noel. Let's find you some shade, eh? Once we get him home, we'll find you somewhere cool to rest." He shifted the boy onto one arm, and put his free hand on her head and ruffled her hair. "We can't keep the sun off you completely. But we'll do our best."
He gave her a small smile, and walked on, and let the boy's mumbling steer him. Some of the names were ones he had heard in the village.
"We've got this, Noel," he said, hardly louder than the wind.

At the edge of the village, Noel ducked behind a tree to get out of the light. She pulled her cloak over herself, as much of herself as it would cover, and peered out at Kiel from behind the trunk with enormous pleading eyes.
The boy lifted a hand, slowly, and pointed: a cabin, the nearest one to the village gate.
Kiel looked at Noel's eyes, and gave in.
"All right. You stay here. I'll take him home."
She smiled at him, delighted, grateful, and hid herself deeper, and was gone.
The village was waking up. A few people were already out. They were a long way off, but they saw him, and they waved. That was new.
The cabin was a five-minute walk. It was in good repair, and someone inside was clattering cups and plates.
At Yuran's, Caelan followed Serrah out of the door. On the way he gave the elf a nod.
"We'll be outside for a moment. Don't feel lonely while we're gone."
It was a jab. Nobody had ever enjoyed being left alone as much as Ninthalarion did.
"I won't," said Ninthalarion, before the door shut.
Outside, the sun was on the snow, and the cold was the kind you could bear. Serrah sat down on the step with her breakfast in her lap and began to eat it without noticing what it was.
Caelan stood a little way off, looking out at the other houses in the quiet morning.
"Thank you for agreeing to it," he said. "I know it wasn't easy."
"Yeah," said Serrah. "Don't mention it."
She looked at the horizon, and wondered how her life had got so far out of hand in just a few days.
Caelan sat down beside her. For a while he only watched the village go about its morning.

"Moments like this," he said. "Peace. People comfortable with each other. That's what I want. An age when people can live in harmony. To make a difference in their lives. To fight for the ones who can't fight, and protect the things they live by."
There was something sad in the way he said it. He clasped his hands and leaned his elbows on his knees.
Serrah put a bit of cheese in her mouth.
"Why?" she said. "Why are you doing all of this?"
The door of the cabin opened.
An old woman stood there with a warm smile and a mug in her hand, ready to say good morning to whoever it was. Then she saw who Kiel was holding.
The mug hit the floor with a clang of tin.
"What? *Erik?*"
At the table inside, heads turned.
"What's up, Ma? What are you..."
She was already on the boy. She touched his face, his hair, his face again, to be sure he was real.
"It's Erik!" she was shouting. "It's Erik!"

There were seven of them at that table, and they all stood up, at all different speeds, and then Kiel was surrounded: people asking questions, people crying, a man leaping straight up in the air. Someone took his arm and pulled him in over the doorstep.
The boy smiled at them all, weakly. He was glad. He was relieved. But there was a question in his eyes that he did not know how to ask.
"Given the choice," said Caelan, "between letting other people's suffering go on, or standing beside them and giving them a fighting chance, I choose the second. It's the right thing to do."
His face went red as he said it. It sounded grander out loud than it did in his head. But it was the truth, and it was what moved him.
Serrah turned and looked at him.
"Really? That's it?"

"That's it. Something as simple as that. If I can do that, and inspire even one person, the world might change one day." He laughed, and smiled at her. It was a moment of honesty between the two of them, and he knew it. "It's as simple as that."
"You're telling me," said Serrah, "that you came all this way just to be *nice?* Can't you be nice somewhere else? You look like you're from far away. Don't they need you over there?"
She looked out over the village, slowly, gathering her thoughts.

"This is just a little mining town that nobody really cares about. I've heard there are cities. With big buildings. And people. More people. Important people, even. I'm sure, very sure, you could help them, and get more done there. Don't you think?" She looked down at her dried meat and her crumbs of cheese. "Not that I'm complaining. I really do appreciate you coming all this way. I just don't understand it."
"That's what they told me, where I come from," said Caelan. "Be nice somewhere else. They don't take kindly to someone trying to change the way the world is."
He thought of all the times he had taken the side of someone the strong and the rich were picking on.

"I did my share of 'nice' there. Enough that the people there can fend for themselves now. But places like this, where the ones who could make a difference choose not to care, and the ones who would push others down are waiting for their first chance, those are the places that need me most. And I'll go to them gladly." He smiled at her. "Maybe one day you'll come with me, and be nice in other places like Hadari."
He looked out at the frozen country around them, the middle of nowhere, where he had found someone as strong as Serrah.

Inside the cabin it was warm. The door had shut out the cold, and the room smelled of a good breakfast. Kiel stood in the middle of the shouting and the crying and the joy, and let it go past him, and watched.
He watched the boy. Erik was smiling. But Kiel had seen that look before, in people who had woken up somewhere they did not remember going to sleep.

Every so often Kiel looked at the window, toward the trees at the edge of the village, where a small figure was hiding from the light. He wished she could see this. A family that had lost a son, and got him back. All of this was hers.
He stepped back, a little at a time, until he was at the edge of the room, and then at the door. Nobody saw him go. He left them their morning.
He walked back toward the trees, to the girl who had done all of it and did not like the sun, and wondered how much of it she would still remember by noon.

chapters.title: Silverstar's Desire
paragraphs: Caelan had a deer half-skinned on the block behind the hunters' hut when the forest began to die.

It went quietly. There was no wind and no sound, only a change in the color of things, as if someone had drawn a wet cloth across a painting. The pines nearest the hut greyed at the tips. The grey ran down the needles and into the bark, and the bark split, and the needles came down all at once, a dry rain that hissed on the snow.
He was running before he had decided to. Serrah had gone into the wood that morning, and Serrah did not come back from anything just because she was told to.

He found her in the middle of it, turning in a slow circle while the trees around her went to ash-colored sticks. He picked her up without asking. She weighed nothing, and she fought like a sack of cats.

"Put me down!" She kicked, and got a fistful of his collar, and pulled. "I know who did this. It's obviously Noel, you idiot! And you're not taking me anywhere. I'll sort this out myself if I have to bite your throat out. I'm just as involved as you are, and I'm not a child!"

Caelan did not answer. He carried her out of the grey, uphill, to a clearing they had camped in before, where the snow was still white and the trees still green. Only there did he set her on her feet.

"No, you're not a child," he said. "But I wasn't going to watch you turn the same as those trees. You're involved, and keeping you alive is my concern." He looked down the slope at the dying wood. "Let's look into this with a cool head."
Serrah looked at him. Then, in one movement, she pulled his hunting knife out of its sheath at his belt.
"Fine. I'm cool. Let's go where things are dying the fastest. Whatever."
She pointed the knife down the hill and set off without waiting for him.
"If we do this," Caelan called after her, "you follow my lead, and you do as I say. If your life is in danger, I'll carry you back again, and I won't ask."
"I do what I want, thank you," said Serrah, "with or without your permission," and walked faster.

He could have caught her. Instead he lengthened his stride until he was walking beside her, and found, to his own surprise, that he liked her for it. She did not back down. Not from the forest, and not from him.

The grey had spread a long way. Caelan read it the way he read a field before a fight: where the dead branches were thickest, where the ground had gone pale, which way the dying leaned. It all leaned the same way, down toward the old cave.
"Be ready for anything," he said, and hoped Noel was safe with Kiel.
Kiel heard Serrah before he saw anything. There was no mistaking that voice. It carried through the dead trees like a dropped pan.
Noel lifted her head from his shoulder. He had been carrying her for the last mile, since she had walked into her third tree; she weighed less than his pack.
"It's Serrah," he said. "Don't worry about it." He gave her shoulder a squeeze and kept walking. "Whatever this is, we didn't cause it. But we should find out what did."

He did not say the rest: that a forest dying in an afternoon, the week after a girl with no breath in her had brought back a boy the town below had given up for lost, was the kind of thing a town would want to blame on someone. He was not going to let it be her.

They came out on a ledge above the cave. Two months they had spent around this cave. Two months the air coming out of it had smelled like something rotting in a closed room. Today the air was clean. Whatever had lived in it, whatever had soaked into the stone around it, was gone, as if it had never been.
Noel stiffened in his arms. Her one eye went wide, and she pointed, hard, at the cave mouth.
"W-wait. That's mine!"
Someone was walking out of the dark, and he had to duck to do it.

He was a little over two meters of Frost Elf, straight as a mast, white hair braided down past his knees. The last time Kiel had seen him he had been grey and shaking, barely able to stand. Now there was nothing wrong with his walk at all. He wore a pelt and nothing else, and in one huge hand, like a twig, he carried Noel's walking stick.
Kiel shifted her behind his shoulder.
"Stay close, Noel," he said, low.
His other hand had already found his sword.
Ninthalarion gave the stick a shake. The opal sheen that covered it slid off the wood, ran up his arm into the turquoise runes on his skin, and was gone. The stick was dull, stale white again.
He looked at Kiel. He raised one eyebrow.
"What."
He glanced back at the cave, and then at Kiel again, as if explaining something to a slow dog.

"All the yammering in that town about people being revived was driving me mad. So I decided to finish my work, before someone," and here he looked at Noel, "felt the urge to bring back more people, make more noise, and pull something from beyond the veil that has no business being here."

Up on the slope, Serrah had reached a rock above the cave with Caelan a step behind her. She saw the Frost Elf, and she went red to the ears. That elf. She had been afraid of his kind every day of her life, and she was done with it. She filled her lungs.
"YOU DID THIS? FOR FU"
Ninthalarion snapped his fingers. His runes flickered.
The snow under Serrah's boots was gone.

She dropped. Caelan's hand closed on hers before he knew he had moved, and then they were both sliding, down the slope in a spray of white, Caelan's body twisting to take the rocks so that she would not. At the bottom he put himself between her and the cave, and she clung to him like a wet cat and spat snow.
"What," said Caelan, and his voice rang off the cliff, "is the meaning of this?"
Ninthalarion had not looked away from Kiel and Noel.
"You're welcome," he said, "for all of my work."
Then he did turn, slowly, and gave the other two the look of a man interrupted at his supper.
"She's loud, and I'm tired. A fall that short never hurt anyone."

Caelan helped Serrah to her feet and kept hold of her hand, and walked her toward Kiel. He did not hurry. He had heard the stories this whole coast told about Frost Elves, and he did not intend to let one of them watch him hurry.
"The forest is dying," he said. "What do you know about it?"
Ninthalarion twirled the stick once.

"That is the advantage of a staff of Silverstar's Desire. I needed my strength back to finish my work and leave as soon as possible." His eyes went to Noel, who had slipped out from behind Kiel and was trying to get around him toward the cave, mostly by falling over. "What I do not understand is how *she* came to have it. Or how she can use it at all."
Kiel had not moved. Something had come into his face that Caelan had seen before, on hunts, at the moment the quarry turned.
"Your work," said Kiel. "You walk around like you saved the world, and all you do is wreck what's in front of you. Keep your thanks. We didn't need your help."

"Yes. My work." The elf's voice did not rise. "Without it, the Xylothara would have laid this land waste before you were born. It cost me my life." The air turned colder, all at once, the way it does when a door opens onto winter. "And if you want to talk about reckless things, why don't we talk about the people you and your friends have been bringing back from the dead?"
Snow began to lift off the ground around them, and turn in the wind, and come down as hail.
"Ninthalarion!" Caelan stepped forward. "We don't have to do this. Give Noel her stick back. Giving people a second chance, like the one you got, isn't reckless. You don't have to do this."
"Do what?" The elf seemed honestly puzzled. "And surely, leaving a thing like this with an undead who has the mind of a child is not the wisest plan."
"My specialty," said Kiel, "is killing pompous Frost Elves. Don't tempt me."
But his shoulders had come down a little. He could see it as well as Caelan could: the elf had not come out of that cave looking for a fight. He had come out because he was finished in there.
"Caelan's right," Kiel said. "We don't have to do this. You're at a disadvantage here. Give the staff back to Noel, and we all walk away."

"Why should I? It is a dangerous thing in the wrong hands, and its owner leaves it lying about in front of me. That is not responsible." Ninthalarion folded his arms, and the ground around him grew. In the time it took to blink, a ring of ice spikes stood around him, clear as glass, taller than Caelan. His runes and his left eye shone the same turquoise. "And no. I am not at a disadvantage against you, child. I have everything I would need to kill you."
He leaned back against one of the spikes.
"But I won't. The man in red made me swear an oath not to harm you or your little band."
Kiel laughed, short and low.
"Me neither," he said. "See, you're standing in my trap."

Caelan looked, and saw it then, the way you only see a snare after someone points: scratches in the rock that were not frost, a line in the snow too straight to be wind, small marks cut into the stones around the cave mouth, sigils and runes worked into the ground in a wide ring. Kiel had not been idle for two months.
"Who do you think killed the spider?" Kiel said. "And unlike some people, I don't mind dying, if I take you with me."

"YOUR HANDS ARE NOT MEANT FOR IT!" Caelan had not known he was going to shout. "Give back what isn't yours. She doesn't do what she does out of malice, or greed. She cares for the ones who die before they're ready. Calling her a child is an insult." The cold had Serrah shaking against him; he unpinned his fur-lined cloak and put it around her shoulders. "Keep this on. It'll keep you warm, even in this."
Then he walked forward until he stood beside Kiel.

"We each have our duty. I believe yours is a noble one. If it weren't for you, whatever lived in that cave would have won." His cape lifted and snapped in the wind. "My duty is to protect these people from tyrants, and from anyone who takes power that isn't theirs."
"Not a child?" said Ninthalarion.
He looked at Noel. She had nearly reached the cave. She tripped on nothing, fell flat on her face in the snow, picked herself up, took two steps, and fell again.
He looked back at the two men. He did not say anything. He did not need to.
"Also, son of man," he went on, "you killed a Xylothara with a fraction of its old strength left. With help, I am told."

"Not my fault you did a lousy job," said Kiel. "And that's my point. I didn't even need the spells I'd laid for it." He spread his arms at the field of hidden marks around them. "I was looking forward to fighting you. But I see now there's not much you can do naked and unarmed. Give me the staff, and stop wasting my time."

"It is not my fault," said Ninthalarion, and for the first time he raised his voice, "that a pack of ignorant humans wore through my wards and tampered with my seals!" His runes blazed. The temperature fell again, and the wind came up white and blinding. "Of course you did not need a single spell. It was that weak. And you still needed the help of a dead child. Congratulations." He did not leave his ring of ice. "I do not need clothes, or armor, or metal, to finish you. And I am not a man who lets a disaster happen because a few strangers ask him to trust an undead girl with a mind like that."
He took the stick in both hands. In his grip it looked like a matchstick.
"I will not fight you. I keep my oaths. But it might be best if there were nothing left to argue over. Breaking it does not sound like a bad idea."
He began to bend it.
Noel stopped in the snow. Her eye went wide.
"Please don't," she said. "Please don't. It's mine. I need it. Please."
Kiel snapped his fingers.

It rang out over the snow like a small bell, and every spike of ice around the cave mouth slumped into water at once. The wind dropped. Warmth came up out of the ground, from the ring of marks Kiel had cut into the rock, and pressed the cold back, and where it reached, the elf's magic simply stopped.

"You're a fool," said Kiel. "Go on. Make me do it." He raised his hand again, fingers ready. "This isn't my first time dealing with Frost Elves. You're all the same. And I've killed more than monsters. I've learned the real monsters usually have a name, and a surname." He let that sit. "You had an afternoon to prepare. I've had two months."
Caelan did not wait to see who would move first.

He ran at the elf, used one of those great legs as a step, and went up. His bow swung and cracked across the stick and knocked it loose toward Noel; his other hand shoved the tattooed arm the other way.
"You're hurting her!" he shouted, in the air.
"Of course I am not, don't be ridiculous!"
The stick flew. But the elf's fist had already closed, and before it left his grip he crushed a small piece of it to glitter.
It made a sound like a pane of glass giving way.
Noel stopped asking.
She stood very still in the snow. She blinked twice. Then she lifted a hand and touched her face, where a crack had opened from her brow to her jaw, fine and bright, as if she were made of glass.
Ninthalarion stared at her. He had stopped fighting entirely.
Caelan reached her first. He took her hand and lowered her into his arms, and she let him, the way a doll lets you.
"Noel," he said. "Noel."
Her face, close up, was not skin any more along that crack. It had the same faint sheen the stick had.
"I feel," she said, very small. "Ah. Where am I?"
"I didn't mean that," said Ninthalarion, behind them. "That was not my intention."
Caelan stood up with her in his arms. He did not look at the elf yet. He looked at her.

"You'll regret the day your pride clouded your judgment," he said, quietly. "We tried to reason with you, again and again. What kind of grown man torments someone who doesn't know any better? If a child doesn't know better, you teach them. In time, they do better." He carried her across the snow to Serrah. "You're with friends, Noel. You're with friends."
He put her into Serrah's arms. "Please. Look after her."

Serrah, shivering under his cloak, held Noel the way you hold something you have been handed and do not know where to put. She reached out, slowly, and touched one of the cracks. Noel flinched and made a small sound.
Kiel had not moved since the stick broke. Now he did. He walked toward the elf with his hand on his sword, and when he spoke it was barely louder than the wind.
"Ninthalarion. You've crossed a line you don't get to step back over. You've made an enemy today."
The elf did not answer him. He was looking at the ground.

He had made a mess of it, and he knew it. He had broken an oath, or near enough, and he did not know how. He did not know how a stick could hurt a girl. All around his feet, in the snow, lay the glitter he had crushed it into, and the wind was picking up.
He knelt and began to gather it.
"Are you going to fight me," he said, without looking up, "or are you going to help me pick these up before the wind takes them, and we can never fix her? Come on. I think I can mend this."
Kiel stopped. For a moment he only looked at him. Then something went out of his shoulders, and he laughed, a short, sour sound.

"You're really something. You break the kid, then ask for help fixing her? That's the worst-timed request I've ever heard." He looked past the elf, at Noel in Serrah's arms. "But I'll be damned before I turn my back on her now."
He crouched beside the elf in the snow.
"Just remember, frosty. We're not done. Not by a long way."
"Ah," said Ninthalarion, "*now* she is a child. A minute ago she was responsible enough to carry a dangerous artifact. You change your story when it suits you."

Caelan had come back. He pulled off his gloves and went down on his knees at the place where he had caught the stick, and began to pick through the snow for splinters, with his fingers going red, and his body turned into the wind to keep it off the shards.
"Spirits we cannot see," he said, under his breath, "you who are always with her. Help us now, as she has helped you, when she eased your rage, and your grief at dying before your time."

"There are no spirits here," said Ninthalarion. "I exorcised them all." He tried very hard not to roll his eyes. He held out a cupped handful of glitter to Kiel. "Keep these. You can stab me later. Not now. It would be a shame, when I doubt you even know what the staff is made of."
"Yeah, yeah," said Kiel, and took them.
"I want to see how you mean to put this right," said Caelan, and brought his own handful, held shut against the wind.
"With magic," said Ninthalarion. "Obviously."
"Don't worry," said Kiel. "Nobody thought you'd use a hammer and nails." He snapped his fingers again, and the warmth went back into the ground, and the ward was gone.
"Good."

The elf raised his tattooed hand, and ice grew out of his palm, clear as water, and he began to feed the shards into it one by one, moving them inside the ice with small turns of his fingers until two of them touched. Turquoise light went through his runes. When it faded, the two were one piece.
It took a long time. Caelan stood back and watched every moment of it. Kiel stood closer, and did not take his eyes off the elf's hands.
At last Ninthalarion let the ice go, and it fell away, and what was left in his palm was a small piece of white wood, whole.
"Now we join it to the rest. Hand it over."
Caelan did not hand it over. He took the mended piece out of the elf's palm, and the stick, and fitted them himself. The wood glowed as it closed, and was one.
"This belongs to Noel," he said. "If you ever try anything like this again, I will never forgive you. You'll wish you hadn't come back the second time."
He went to Serrah and knelt, and laid the stick in Noel's small hand, and closed her fingers around it.

Serrah had been watching Noel's face the whole time. Under the cracks, where she had expected stillness, there were tiny movements, like ice settling on a pond. Now they quickened. The bright lines began to draw together, slowly, a shard at a time. Noel winced each time one moved.
Caelan put his thumb to her cheek, where there were frozen tears, and they melted.
"Noel," he said. "Noel."
"I feel woozy," said Noel.

Her hair was changing while they watched. There had always been a little black left in it, under the white. Now the black was going, strand by strand, as if the mending were being paid for out of it. When the last of it was white, the mending slowed almost to nothing.
"I," said Noel. "Who are you? I'm tired."
She mumbled something none of them could follow, and turned over, and made herself comfortable in Serrah's arms, and was asleep.
Caelan put his arms around the two of them and held on. "Thank the stars," he said.

Serrah, wrapped in his cloak, with Noel asleep against her and a knight hugging her, sat very still. After a while she patted him on the back. Then she patted Noel. Then, because it seemed only fair, she patted him again.
"All right, frost elf," said Kiel. "You've done your part. Now it's time for answers. You owe us that much."
Ninthalarion had sat down on a rock. He looked as disdainful as ever, but somewhat less so than before.
"Ask. I warn you, I do not have every answer you want, and I promise nothing about how true my memory is."
"The staff. Silverstar's Desire. You said it's tied to her. Explain."

"I think it is clear to everyone here that I had no idea breaking it would do the same to her." The elf pinched the bridge of his nose. "Frankly, it baffles me. And it is not a staff. It is quite literally a stick. I had a staff made from the same tree, in my first life."
He closed his eyes, as if reading something written on the inside of them.

"Silverstar's Desire is a tree. The Elders said such trees fell from the heavens, so they were called stars. They are silver. And above all, they take in the life of everything they touch. Some said that is why the land around them is barren: the tree's hunger for more." He opened his eyes. "Silver. Star's. Desire. Any questions?"

"I've never heard of such a tree," said Caelan. "And I've held that stick. It never took any strength from me. So it must be the wielder who bends it to their will?" He was quiet a moment. "A silver star that fell from the sky, and wants to rise and shine again. To get back up, it steals from everything it meets."
Ninthalarion looked at him the way one looks at a man who has started to sing in a meeting, and went on.

"The living tree takes, and cares nothing for anyone. Dead, as a branch, or as dust," and he lifted his tattooed arm, and for a moment his face was somewhere else entirely, "it can be useful. It lets you restore yourself by taking from others. But only those ingrained with its shards or its dust can use it, because the wood believes it is one with them. I was infused with its glitter. It was a harrowing thing. It marked my body, and something deeper than my body." He looked at Noel. "Your friend I do not understand. Why her face should become part of a stick, I cannot tell you."
"Does it take from the one holding it?" said Kiel. "Could it have taken something from her? Her memories?"
"It can take from the wielder, if they are careless. Memories?" A shrug. "I would expect it to take from the body before the mind. But what do I know."
"How do you even make a staff from a tree like that?" said Kiel. "And why would anyone want to?"
"Very, very carefully. No touching it. Usually no magic, either. It is all done with metal tools, things that are not alive and never were."
"Have you seen one of these trees?" said Caelan. "Touched one?"
"Seen one, from far off. I am no craftsman. I had no need to go near it."
"And the forest," said Kiel. "Did you eat the whole thing, or what?"
The elf looked at them both, with the expression of a man who knows his answer will not be popular.

"I took back all of my strength with it, at the cost of a fair part of the forest's life. Now do you see why I did not like leaving it lying about? I know how to use it. Someone else could have drained everything to sand: the forest, and that little town as well."
"So your carelessness nearly doomed us all," said Kiel. There was no heat in it.

"It did not, and it was not carelessness." The elf was offended. "I took what I judged would cost the area least. Plants. I made sure it would not touch animals or people. I know what I am doing." He sniffed. "Those humans will be fine. They are already talking about going back down the mines and trading with the other towns. It will be a small setback, at most."
"It was still reckless," said Caelan. "People here live off that forest."
The elf did not answer that.
"What will you do now?" Caelan asked. "Now that you've got your strength back? With the Xylothara dead, there's nothing to keep you here."
"I will," said Ninthalarion, and stopped. "Continue my work, I suppose."
He said it with perfect confidence, and looked away while he said it. Caelan had spent years watching people, and he saw the pause.
He closed his eyes, and thought, and opened them.

"My plan is to travel with Noel and help her get her memories back. If she's tied to Silverstar's Desire, we follow that. You're capable, and you know things none of us do." He looked at Kiel, and waited.

Kiel took his time. "As much as I hate to say it," he said at last, "we could use what he knows. But there are rules. This isn't about what you want, or what we want. It's about Noel. If you're not in it for her, there's no place for you."
Ninthalarion looked from one of them to the other, and waited for someone to laugh.
Nobody did.
"This is a joke," he said.
"I can't think of anything better for you to do," said Caelan. "You despise the people in that town, and there isn't another soul out here."
"No joke, frosty," said Kiel. "You've got knowledge we need, and we've got a road that needs it. Your call. In or out?"
"And why should I care about any of this, other than stepping in if the stick is misused?"
Kiel looked at him for a while before he answered.

"Because it isn't only about Noel. The world changed while you were away. Forests you'd remember have been cut down to feed fires. Villages of a hundred are cities of thousands now, and they spread over the land like mold on bread. The people driving it are nobles and saints, and they call their greed virtue and their cruelty justice. The real monsters don't hide in the wild any more. They walk around in good coats." He shrugged. "In every age, they say, one great evil rises. This age has dozens. And it's not just the living world at stake. I don't think you care about money, or about people much. But I'd bet you care about that."
The elf stared back at him. It was plain he was trying to decide whether any of it was true. It was harder to see that some part of him had already decided.
"Have the orcs been wiped out?" he said at last. "Completely?"
"There are orcs on plenty of the islands," said Caelan. "But there are crueler things than orcs."
"They're still around," said Kiel. "And they have long memories. They tell their whole history out loud, every night, so nobody forgets it."
For a long moment Ninthalarion said nothing at all. Then he let out a breath, and nodded.

"Very well. But the moment I wish to leave, or go my own way, I will. And an orc seen is an orc killed." He stood, and the two men had to tip their heads back to keep looking at him. "And I want to leave this disgusting little town as soon as possible. And do not expect me to babysit any of you."
The part about the orcs sat badly with Caelan. He let it sit, for now.

"Then we're in this together," he said, "until we're not." He looked at Serrah, and back at the elf. "You're free to go whenever you choose. That goes for you too, Kiel. Our roads have crossed, and we'll walk them together while it's the same road." He glanced at Noel, asleep, the stick still in her fist. "We can talk about the rest on the way. I had a deer half-skinned when the forest started dying." He gave the elf a long look. "We'll stop at the hunters' hut and finish it for dinner."
Kiel dusted off his knees and gave Serrah a hand up. Then he bent and gathered Noel up, stick and all; she weighed no more than she ever had.

"Well, I'm not one to turn down a good meal," he said, and grinned at the elf, as if the last hour had been a friendly argument about the weather. "Let's go, then. Come on! Let's not keep dinner waiting."
He set off without looking back to see whether anyone followed. They did.
Serrah walked at the back, in a knight's cloak that came down to her ankles, holding a hunting knife she had not used, and wondered what in the world she had just been roped into.
At the front, Ninthalarion stopped once, and looked back over his shoulder at a stretch of empty snow, the way a man looks at someone who has made him promise something.
Then he followed them down the hill.
